signal.title: [NETPATH-1118] Add baseline dynamic tests for CNM
signal.text: <!--Please give us some feedback on your experience writing this PR ! https://app.datadoghq.com/forms/43db4c02-6837-400c-8083-692e141b1b88 !--> ### What does this PR do? Adds opt-in baseline Dynamic Tests for Cloud Network Monitoring. Baseline mode observes eligible CNM traffic over a bounded window, selects up to five representative high-volume paths per Agent, and runs each winner once. #### Product contract - Baseline is a best-effort, automatically curated preview of Network Path. It does not guarantee coverage for a particular connection or destination. - The budget is per Agent: each completed window produces at most five baseline test runs. - Baseline favors stable, important traffic in v1. Diversity, rotation, and diagnostic-signal prioritization are intentionally deferred. - Standard connection-monitoring Dynamic Tests take precedence when enabled. #### Window lifecycle - The first window after baseline starts is five minutes to reduce time to first value. - Later windows are one hour. This cadence is intentionally separate from `network_path.collector.pathtest_interval`, which continues to control recurring Network Path tests. - Candidate ranking is updated continuously as CNM snapshots arrive. Admission is intentionally streaming: a periodic flush may split a concurrently processed snapshot across adjacent windows. This is a known and accepted limitation. - At each boundary, the final winners are submitted once and selection state is reset for the next window. #### Selection - Eligibility and filtering remain upstream. Baseline consumes already-admitted paths without depending on whether built-in, local, or Remote Configuration filtering admitted them. - Observations use the collector's existing normalized path identity: origin, namespace, hostname or IP, effective port, protocol, and source container ID. - A path's score is cumulative sent plus received bytes observed during the window. - Selection uses a weighted Space-Saving heavy-hitter estimator with a fixed 32-candidate set, keeping memory bounded independently of connection count. - Stable path identity provides deterministic tie-breaking. #### Execution - Winners are one-shot baseline executions rather than recurring TTL-backed contexts. - Existing queues, workers, concurrency controls, and rate limits remain shared with other Network Path tests. - A queue drop, rate-limit rejection, or execution failure does not restore the slot, promote another candidate, or trigger catch-up work. - Successful results carry `dynamic_test_profile: "baseline"`. ### Motivation Selecting paths independently from each CNM snapshot can accumulate recurring contexts and produce unstable coverage. Windowed heavy-hitter selection gives baseline a predictable contract: observe traffic over a meaningful period, choose up to five stable high-volume paths, and run each once. ### Test coverage requirements Comprehensive coverage is an acceptance requirement for this change. Tests must cover: - cumulative sent-plus-received byte ranking across multiple snapshots and repeated paths; - the five-minute bootstrap window, subsequent hourly windows, streaming boundary rollover, the accepted adjacent-window snapshot split, reset behavior, partial sets, and empty windows; - bounded candidate memory, heavy-hitter retention, deterministic ties, and overflow-safe accumulation; - the fixed baseline cadence, independence from `pathtest_interval`, and Standard Dynamic Tests precedence; - at-most-five one-shot submissions, including no replacement or retry after input-queue pressure or rate limiting; - preservation of filtering/Remote Configuration provenance and baseline payload attribution; - byte propagation from both CNM connection producers; - race safety for selector and store lifecycle changes; - a packaged-Agent E2E path through CNM traffic, system-probe traceroute, payload encoding, and fakeintake delivery. ### Describe how you validated your changes - `bazel test //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl:impl_test //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl/common:common_test //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl/pathteststore:pathteststore_test //comp/rdnsquerier/impl:impl_test //pkg/config/setup:setup_test //pkg/networkpath/payload:payload_test` - `bazel test --config=gorace //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl:impl_test //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl/pathteststore:pathteststore_test` - `bazel coverage //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl:impl_test //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl/pathteststore:pathteststore_test --combined_report=lcov` (100% line coverage for `baseline.go`; 97.5% for `pathteststore.go`) - `bazel build //test/new-e2e/tests/netpath/dynamic-tests:dynamic-tests_test` The live AWS E2E has not yet been run. A passing packaged-Agent E2E is required before merge; its test binary compiles and CI wiring runs the netpath E2E job for the affected implementation paths. Local `dda inv` lint/test commands could not start because the internal Go toolchain mirror was not resolvable. Bazel validation above completed successfully. ### Additional Notes - Baseline uses a fixed five-test hourly budget, separate from `pathtest_interval`, so preview volume stays predictable without changing standard or NetFlow cadence. - The two connection-adapter paths are included in the netpath E2E change rules so byte-propagation changes continue to exercise this coverage. - This PR targets `main` directly and is not stacked on #54938.

signal.title: Reject unresolved secret handles on the NPM direct-send path
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds `endpoint.CheckAPIKeysResolved` and calls it from `sender.New` (`pkg/network/sender/sender_linux.go`), so that when `network_config.direct_send` is enabled and `api_key` is still an unresolved `ENC[...]` secret handle, the NPM direct sender refuses to start and says why: ``` error creating module network_tracer: create direct sender: api_key is an unresolved secret handle ("ENC[...]"): this process can not resolve secret handles and expects to receive them from the core agent already resolved ``` The check also covers `process_config.additional_endpoints`, since those keys come from the same config and are equally likely to be secret-backed. ### Motivation NTWK-817. A customer set `api_key` via the secret backend (`ENC[k8s_secret@...]`) and enabled `network_config.direct_send`. CNM data never arrived, and nothing in the logs pointed at the cause. What was happening: system-probe wires the **no-op** secrets component (`secretsnoopfx.Module()` in `cmd/system-probe/subcommands/run/command.go`), so it cannot resolve secret handles itself. It only ever receives resolved values from the core agent over config sync (`comp/core/configsync`)— both `agent_ipc.config_refresh_interval` and `agent_ipc.port` default to `0` (`pkg/config/setup/all_settings.go`). With config sync off, `config.GetString("api_key")` returned the literal string `ENC[k8s_secret@...]`, and the direct sender passed it straight through as the `Dd-Api-Key` header. Every payload was rejected by the intake, and because the direct sender has no API-key validation (`DisableAPIKeyChecking = true`) there was no error identifying the key as the problem. Silent data loss. This does not make the customer's setup work — it makes the failure legible. The configuration they still need is in the section below. ### Scope of the check, and why it is not in `GetAPIEndpoints` The check is deliberately **not** inside `GetAPIEndpoints`, even though that is where the API key is read. `module.FactoryDependencies` (`pkg/system-probe/api/module/common.go`) declares `ConnectionsForwarder connectionsforwarder.Component` as a **non-optional** field, and `startSystemProbe` takes that struct — so Fx constructs `connectionsforwarder` on **every** system-probe start regardless of `direct_send`, and its constructor calls `GetAPIEndpoints` and propagates the error (`comp/forwarder/connectionsforwarder/impl/connectionsforwarder.go`). Putting the check there made any system-probe with a secret-backed `api_key` fail to boot outright, taking CWS, USM, and discovery with it — a regression for a large existing population, since that construction was previously a harmless no-op (a forwarder built with an unusable key that nothing read). Keeping the check at the `sender.New` call site means the failure is confined to what is actually broken: the module loader logs the error and skips `network_tracer`, and the rest of system-probe runs normally (`pkg/system-probe/api/module/loader.go`). NPM and USM are both lost, as they share the `network_tracer` module — unavoidable without silently falling back to the process-agent collection path, which would change the deployment topology in response to a config error. Graceful degradation was considered and rejected. `Register()` skips the `/connections` endpoint when `DirectSend` is true, so keeping the module alive without a sender would load eBPF programs, collect connections, and drop them all — the cost of NPM with none of the data, and quietly. ### Customer-facing configuration required for `direct_send` + secrets To make secret-backed `api_key` actually work with `direct_send`, config sync must be enabled so the core agent supplies the resolved value. In `datadog.yaml` (read by both the core agent and system-probe), either TCP: ```yaml agent_ipc: config_refresh_interval: 30 # seconds; must be > 0 port: 5008 # any free port ``` or, preferably in Kubernetes, over a socket: ```yaml agent_ipc: config_refresh_interval: 30 use_socket: true socket_path: /var/run/datadog/agent_ipc.socket # on a volume both containers mount ``` One of the two transports must be set. `comp/core/configsync/impl/module.go` logs `configsync disabled: ...` and does nothing if `config_refresh_interval <= 0`, or if `use_socket` is false and `port <= 0`. Caveats worth flagging to anyone enabling this: - **Startup becomes dependent on core-agent readiness.** system-probe runs config sync with `OnInitSync: true` and a **10-second** deadline (`configSyncTimeout`, retrying every 2s). If the core agent is not yet listening, system-probe fails to start with `failed to sync config at startup, is the core agent listening on '...'`. Where both start together this is a real race. - **`use_socket` needs a shared volume.** The standard Helm chart does not give the two containers a shared writable run directory by default; an explicit `emptyDir` mounted into both is required. - The only alternative is a literal `api_key` in the config system-probe reads, which defeats the point of using a secret backend. This interaction is currently undocumented — `direct_send` has no entry in `pkg/config/example/system-probe_*.yaml.example`, no description in the generated schema, and no coverage under `docs/`. Documentation is intentionally left out of this PR and will be handled separately. ### Describe how you validated your changes Unit: added `endpoints_test.go` covering a plain key, a bare handle, a whitespace-padded handle, a handle in an additional endpoint, and an empty key. `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/process/runner/endpoint` passes; `dda inv linter.go` clean on `pkg/process/runner/endpoint` and `pkg/network/sender`. End-to-end, in a Linux container (arm64, kernel 6.8, CO-RE) with `direct_send: true`, `api_key: ENC[k8s_secret@...]`, `process_config.process_dd_url` pointed at a local stub intake, and no config sync configured: | | before this change | with this change | |---|---|---| | system-probe process | runs but direct sender gets payloads rejected | stays up, socket bound | | `network_tracer` | n/a | `error creating module network_tracer: create direct sender: api_key is an unresolved secret handle ...` | | other modules | none | `discovery` and `event_monitor` both started | | requests reaching intake | payloads sent with `Dd-Api-Key: ENC[...]` | 0 | | `ENC[` observed on the wire | yes | 0 | `dda inv system-probe.build` also verified in the Linux container, since `sender_linux.go` is not compiled on macOS. ### Additional Notes The error message names the offending setting path, so it distinguishes `api_key` from `process_config.additional_endpoints`. The handle itself is included in the message; it is a reference, not a secret value.

signal.title: [ACTP] package and activate par-control
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Packages and activates split-mode PAR on Linux and Windows hosts: - installs `par-control` and process-manager definitions for it and the on-demand executor; - adds Agent package, installer, and Windows executable-resource wiring; - preserves a standard Unix service `PATH` for process-manager children; - adds fake-OPMS support plus Linux and Windows lifecycle/bootstrap E2E suites and CI jobs. Two details about how the definitions delegate to `dd-procmgrd`: - Windows has no console for a service to inherit, so the `par-control` definition redirects `stdout`/`stderr` to `<ETC_ROOT>/logs/par-control.log` instead of the binary managing its own log file. `dd-procmgrd` now creates a missing stdio parent directory rather than silently falling back to inherit on a fresh install. - The PAR definitions set `DD_FLEET_POLICIES_DIR=${DD_CONF_DIR}/managed/datadog-agent/stable`, which `dd-procmgrd` expands from the supervising unit, so a stable or experiment unit selects the matching config tree. Hardcoding the rendered stable path would have made the control plane and executor read stable policies during an experiment while the core Agent read the experiment's. This matches what the DDOT definition already does. Windows keeps reading `fleet_policies_dir` from the registry, as `pkg/config/setup/config_windows.go` does, because there are no experiment services there. Docker and Kubernetes deployments remain monolithic. ### Validation - `dda env dev run -- bazel test //pkg/fleet/installer/packages:packages_test //pkg/fleet/installer/packages/embedded:tmpl_test //pkg/procmgr/rust:dd-procmgrd_test` - `dda inv linter.go --module=test/new-e2e --targets=./tests/privateactionrunner` The installer test now pins the full `DD_FLEET_POLICIES_DIR` value for both definitions; asserting only the key name would not catch a regression to a hardcoded path. Live Linux and Windows E2E execution is left to CI. _Stack 9 of 9; based on #54594._

signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds the authenticated local gRPC channel between `par-control` and the Go executor: - health and readiness checks; - workflow signing-key synchronization that keeps the executor alive while synchronization is in progress without counting it as an active action. The executor's idle tracking gains a distinct activity counter for this, so non-action work suppresses idle exit while `ActiveActions` still reports only running actions; - action dispatch and terminal outcomes; - Unix-socket and Windows named-pipe transports using the Agent IPC certificate; - message limits sized for large action payloads. This layer introduces the crate's generated-bindings module and the local transport helpers, since it is the first one that needs executor protos and mTLS. OPMS polling and orchestration remain in later layers. ### Validation Focused Go and Rust tests cover the protocol, key synchronization and idle interaction, transport, and message limits. Proto changes are Bazel-validated because Cargo and Bazel use separate generated bindings. - `dda env dev run -- bazel test //pkg/privateactionrunner/par-control:par-control_test //pkg/privateactionrunner/executor:executor_test` - `dda env dev run -- env -u PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR cargo test -p par-control` _Stack 5 of 9; based on #54590 and followed by #54592._

signal.title: [BARX-2009] Drop Agent 6 RC tags on Go modules
signal.text: ## Motivation - Agent releases create a nested Go module tag for every release candidate. These tags significantly increase the repository's tag count and add pressure to GitHub and GitLab. Agent 7 already drops creating these RC module tags; this PR applies the same behavior to Agent 6. See the [RFC](https://docs.google.com/document/d/15XFZ4AKy8Yhyruo7zilTR84j5kV1dI5eFBhoEFfGzhI/edit?tab=t.0) for more info. ## Important Note - Agent 6 RC module dependencies use versions backed by RC tags. After removing those tags, the dependencies must use another resolvable version. We use pseudo-versions derived from the release branch commit, ensuring modules in the same RC can consume each other’s changes without creating nested RC tags. ## Changes - Skip nested Go module tag creation for Agent 6 release candidates. - Resolve Agent 6 RC internal module dependencies to canonical pseudo-versions at the current release branch commit. - Cache each resolved pseudo-version while updating module requirements. - Keep final Agent 6 release tags - Document the Agent 6 RC pseudo-version workflow. - Add unit coverage for tag suppression and pseudo-version dependency updates. ## Tests - `dda inv invoke-unit-tests.run --tests=release` (46 tests passed) - `GITLAB_CI=true dda inv linter.python` - `git diff --check`

signal.title: Fix ksm gvk collision
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Fixes a GroupVersionKind (GVK) collision in the Cluster Agent's kube-state-metrics (KSM) custom-resource collection. When two CRDs share the same `Kind` and plural name but belong to different API groups (e.g. `Project`/`projects` in both `artifactory.example.com` and `sonarqube.example.com`), they no longer collide onto a single API client. The KSM custom-resource client map was keyed by the bare plural name (`factory.Name()`, e.g. `"projects"`), which is group-blind. Two same-plural CRDs overwrote each other in the map, so both collectors' reflectors ended up sharing a single dynamic client bound to one group. The reflector for the other group then received objects of an unexpected GVK. Clients are now keyed by their fully-qualified GroupVersionResource on both the populate side (`discoverCustomResources` / `GetCustomResourceClientsAndCollectors`) and the lookup side (`getCustomResourceClient`), via a shared `CustomResourceClientKey` helper. This mirrors upstream KSM's own `CreateCustomResourceClients` keying. ### Motivation Customer escalation [CONS-8512](https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/CONS-8512): a customer collecting custom-resource metrics for two `Project` CRDs in different API groups saw repeated `Unexpected watch event object gvk` errors in the Cluster Agent and incorrect, cross-contaminated project counts. Renaming a CRD is the only current workaround, which the customer cannot adopt. ### Describe how you validated your changes - Added unit tests in `pkg/kubestatemetrics/builder/gvk_collision_test.go`: - `CustomResourceClientKey` produces group-distinct keys for two same-plural CRDs. - Two same-plural/different-group resources each resolve their own client (no overwrite; each store's lookup, driven by its own `ExpectedType`, returns the matching client). - `bazel test //pkg/kubestatemetrics/builder:builder_test_dca` → PASSED. - `dda inv test` for `pkg/collector/corechecks/cluster/ksm/...` and `pkg/kubestatemetrics/builder/...` pass; `go vet` clean. ### Additional Notes - Agent-side only — no changes to the vendored/forked kube-state-metrics. - The populate and lookup sides both route through `util.GVRFromType(f.Name(), f.ExpectedType())`, so their keys are guaranteed to agree. Falls back to the plural name when a GVR cannot be derived, matching upstream KSM behavior. - Related upstream issue (separate manifestation in the standalone KSM binary): kubernetes/kube-state-metrics#2015. [CONS-8512]: https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/CONS-8512?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNWRkNTljNzYxNjVmNDY3MDlhMDU5Y2ZhYzA5YTRkZjUiLCJwIjoiZ2l0aHViLWNvbS1KU1cifQ

signal.title: ci(ddot): make otel apt mirror resilient to slow mirrors
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Makes the apt package-mirror config in `Dockerfiles/agent-ddot/Dockerfile.agent-otel` (used by `docker_image_build_otel`) resilient to *slow* mirrors, by giving apt real per-request failover: - Rewrites the deb822 `URIs:` fields in `ubuntu.sources` to an ordered multi-URI list (`us-west-2`, `archive.ubuntu.com`, `mirror.leaseweb.net`) so apt fails over to the next mirror on error. - Drops `us-east-1` (the chronically-slow mirror in the timeout logs). - `Acquire::Retries "1"` + 10s timeout so a slow mirror becomes a fast error that triggers failover. ### Motivation `docker_image_build_otel` intermittently timed out (~3% of runs, across many branches). The build spent its whole wall-clock in `apt-get install build-essential` against a congested `us-east-1` mirror. A first attempt (mirror+file peer list + Acquire timeout) did **not** fix it: apt's `mirror` method sticks to one mirror per invocation and only fails over when it's fully unreachable, so a slow-but-reachable `us-east-1` kept timing out and `Acquire::Retries` retried the same URI to the job timeout. This PR switches to explicit ordered `URIs:` for genuine per-request failover. ### Describe how you validated your changes - CI Visibility + job logs isolated mirror throughput as the only variable (successful same-commit runs finished in 16-21m). - Validated the `sed` `URIs:` rewrite against the default noble `ubuntu.sources`. - CI will exercise the real build here. ### Additional Notes The same fix is applied to the other CI Dockerfiles in #55119. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: AGENT-16721: Support multi formats of pan-os config
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Makes the built-in `pan-os` NCM profile accept both output formats that PAN-OS `show config running` can return: - **Angle-bracket XML** (`<config>...</config>`) — already supported. - **Curly-brace hierarchical** (`config { ... }`) — returned by newer PAN-OS in operational mode, where `set cli config-output-format xml` only affects configuration-mode `show`. Changes in `pkg/networkconfigmanagement/profile/default_profiles.go`: - `GetRunning` validator: `(?s)<config.*</config>` → `(?s)(<config.*</config>|config\s*\{)` - Adds a second redaction rule so the `phash` password hash is scrubbed in the curly-brace format (`phash $5$...;`) in addition to the XML form (`<phash>...</phash>`). Adds `Test_PanOSGetRunningValidator` and `Test_PanOSRedaction` covering both formats — the validator regex was previously untested for pan-os. ### Motivation [AGENT-16721](https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/AGENT-16721) (Zendesk 2965009). A customer's Palo Alto firewall returns curly-brace output from `show config running`, so the profile's XML-only validator (`(?s)<config.*</config>`) never matched and every NCM check failed with `does not match required regex` — even though SSH auth and profile selection succeeded. Same root-cause class as the archived AGENT-16369. The redaction change is required alongside the validator fix: without it, the newly-collected curly-brace configs would ship the admin password hash in cleartext, since the existing `<phash>...</phash>` rule does not match `phash $5$...;`. ### Describe how you validated your changes `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/networkconfigmanagement/profile/` — all 22 tests pass, including: - `Test_PanOSGetRunningValidator` — XML and curly-brace inputs validate; error strings and empty output are rejected. - `Test_PanOSRedaction` — `phash` is scrubbed in both formats (asserts the raw hash no longer appears in the redacted output). - `Test_DefaultProfiles_Running` — existing XML fixture still passes unchanged. - Tested internally with a Palo Alto Firewall [AGENT-16721]: https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/AGENT-16721?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNWRkNTljNzYxNjVmNDY3MDlhMDU5Y2ZhYzA5YTRkZjUiLCJwIjoiZ2l0aHViLWNvbS1KU1cifQ

signal.title: fix(installer): embed -nocap systemd unit templates
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Adds `//go:embed` directives for `tmpl/gen/oci-nocap/*.service` and `tmpl/gen/debrpm-nocap/*.service`, and the matching Bazel `embedsrcs` entries, so the `-nocap` systemd unit templates ship inside the installer binary. Adds `embed_test.go`, which enumerates units through the `embed.FS` and asserts `GetSystemdUnit` resolves every unit in both the ambient-capability and `-nocap` variants. ## Motivation This is to address this escalation: https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/AGENT-16750 `GetSystemdUnit` selects the `-nocap` templates on hosts whose kernel does not support ambient capabilities (older than 4.3), but no `//go:embed` directive covered those directories. Unit generation failed at runtime with: ``` failed to write stable units: open tmpl/gen/debrpm-nocap/datadog-agent.service: file does not exist ``` The package manager scriptlet ignores that failure, so the install reported success while the host was left with no Datadog units and `systemctl start datadog-agent` returned `Unit not found`. Both the classic DEB/RPM path and Fleet Automation remote upgrades and config experiments (`oci-nocap`) were affected. The existing tests missed this because they read the template tree from disk instead of from the `embed.FS`, so the templates were always present regardless of the embed directives. ## Verification - `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/fleet/installer/packages/embedded` - 83 tests passed - `bazel test //pkg/fleet/installer/packages/embedded:all` - `embedded_test` and `tmpl_test` passed - The new `TestGetSystemdUnitEmbedsAllVariants` fails on `main` (`file does not exist` for every `-nocap` unit) and passes with this change - `TestGetSystemdUnitSelectsNocapVariant` confirms the `-nocap` unit actually has `AmbientCapabilities=` stripped, not just that it loads ### Known gap, not addressed here `tmpl/datadog-agent-data-plane.service.tmpl` emits `AmbientCapabilities` unconditionally, without the `{{ if .AmbiantCapabilitiesSupported }}` guard its siblings use, so its two variants are byte-identical. That is a pre-existing template defect, out of scope for this fix, and is documented in a comment on the test. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: fix(wlan): do not panic when wlanapi.dll is unavailable on Windows
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Stops the Windows `wlan` check from panicking when `wlanapi.dll` cannot be loaded. `wlanapi.dll` ships with the Windows `Wireless-Networking` feature, which is **not installed by default on Windows Server**. `windows.LazyProc.Call` panics (via `mustFind`) instead of returning an error when it cannot resolve the DLL, so the very first call in `getWlanHandle` blew up. `GetWiFiInfo` now loads the DLL before calling into it, and reports no active Wi-Fi interface (`phyMode: "None"` → WARNING status) when the load fails. A host with no WLAN stack has no Wi-Fi interface to report on, which is a normal server state rather than a collection failure. `LazyDLL.Load` already caches the module handle on success and guards itself with a mutex, so calling it per run costs a single atomic load once the library is present — no `sync.Once` needed, and wrapping it in one would additionally cache the *failure*, which `Load` deliberately does not. Loading per run also means a host that installs `Wireless-Networking` starts reporting on the next check tick with no Agent restart. ### Motivation Jira: [WINA-3050](https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/WINA-3050) Reported crash: the Agent process crashes on Windows Server when the `wlan` check is enabled and there is no Wi-Fi. Reproduced on a Windows Server 2022 VM with no `Wireless-Networking` feature installed (`wlanapi.dll` absent, `wlansvc` not registered), running Agent 7.82.1: ``` panic: The specified module could not be found. golang.org/x/sys/windows.(*LazyProc).mustFind(...) golang.org/x/sys@v0.47.0/windows/dll_windows.go:293 golang.org/x/sys/windows.(*LazyProc).Call(...) golang.org/x/sys@v0.47.0/windows/dll_windows.go:315 +0x59 .../wlan.getWlanHandle() wlan_windows.go:375 .../wlan.getFirstConnectedWlanInfo() wlan_windows.go:468 .../wlan.(*WLANCheck).GetWiFiInfo() wlan_windows.go:516 .../wlan.(*WLANCheck).Run() wlan.go:158 .../check.runCheck(...) command.go:674 ``` Two symptoms depending on the path: - **`agent check wlan`** — hard crash, full panic to stderr, non-zero exit (the CLI path has no recover). - **Long-running agent service** — survives thanks to the recover in `pkg/collector/worker`, but degrades permanently: the panic is recovered and re-logged every 15s, a MEDIUM health-platform issue stays open, and no `system.wlan.*` metrics are ever emitted. ``` ERROR | worker.go:232 | Recovered from panic in check wlan: The specified module could not be found. ERROR | check_logger.go:71 | check:wlan | Error running check: check panicked: ... INFO | Health platform: NEW issue from collector: Check 'wlan' Failed (ISSUE_SEVERITY_MEDIUM) ``` On an Agent older than #49763 (which added the worker recover, so roughly pre-7.75) the service itself would have died outright. Note the trigger is *no WLAN stack*, not *no Wi-Fi network*. A server with the feature installed but not associated to an AP already worked correctly. ### Describe how you validated your changes - Reproduced the original panic on the affected VM (Windows Server 2022, Agent 7.82.1), both via `agent check wlan` and in the running service log. - Added `wlan_windows_test.go` (`windows && test`): with the loader stubbed to fail, `GetWiFiInfo` does not panic and returns `phyMode: "None"` with no error. Deterministic on any runner, including ones that do have the DLL. - `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/collector/corechecks/net/wlan` — 17 tests pass. - `GOOS=windows dda inv linter.go --targets=./pkg/collector/corechecks/net/wlan --build-tags=test` — 0 issues; verified the Windows-only test file is actually typechecked (temporarily injected a type error and confirmed the linter caught it). - `BUILD.bazel` regenerated with `bazel run //:gazelle`, then formatted with `bazel run //bazel/buildifier` (no changes produced). `bazel test //bazel/buildifier:test` passes, so the file is clean in both `diff` and `warn` lint mode. **Verified end-to-end on the affected host.** Installed this PR's pipeline MSI (`pipelines/A7/131968742`, `7.84.0-devel.git.310.3d4ea7b`, SHA256 verified after transfer) on the same Windows Server 2022 VM that reproduced the crash, with `wlanapi.dll` still absent and the same `wlan.d/conf.yaml` in place. | | Before (7.82.1) | After (3d4ea7b) | |---|---|---| | `agent check wlan` | `panic: The specified module could not be found.`, non-zero exit | `Instance ID: wlan [OK]`, **exit code 0** | | Service, per 15s run | 2 ERROR lines + MEDIUM health issue | `Running check...` → `Done running check`, no errors | | New recovered panics after restart | every run | **0** over 75s / 6 runs | | `system.wlan.*` metrics | none emitted | `system.wlan.status = 1` (warning), `reason:interface_inactive` | | Health platform | `Check 'wlan' Failed (ISSUE_SEVERITY_MEDIUM)` | no issue raised | Confirmed the new branch is what executes, rather than the check succeeding for some unrelated reason (`--log-level debug`): ``` DEBUG | (pkg/collector/corechecks/net/wlan/wlan_windows.go:527 in GetWiFiInfo) | Skipping Wi-Fi collection, wlanapi.dll is unavailable: The specified module could not be found. WARN | (pkg/collector/corechecks/net/wlan/wlan.go:179 in Run) | No active Wi-Fi interface detected: PHYMode is none. ``` Same underlying Windows error that used to be the panic, now a debug line and a WARNING status. ### Additional Notes The shipped `wlan.d/conf.yaml.default` carries the `_end_user_device` AD identifier, which normally keeps this check off servers; reproducing required a hand-written `wlan.d/conf.yaml`, which is presumably what the reporting host has. [WINA-3050]: https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/WINA-3050?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNWRkNTljNzYxNjVmNDY3MDlhMDU5Y2ZhYzA5YTRkZjUiLCJwIjoiZ2l0aHViLWNvbS1KU1cifQ

signal.title: fix(windows): don't lock out the domain agent user account on upgrade
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Makes the Windows MSI set `dd-procmgr-service`'s start type to **disabled** when the Agent user password is not available, and back to **demand start** once it is available again. The condition is deliberately narrowed to **domain accounts**: | account type | `isDomainAccount` | `isServiceAccount` | password empty? | start type | |---|---|---|---|---| | domain user, password supplied or from LSA | true | false | no | `Manual` | | **domain user, no password anywhere** | **true** | **false** | **yes** | **`Disabled`** ← the bug | | local user, no password supplied | false | false | no (generated) | `Manual` | | gMSA | – | true | yes | `Manual` | | LocalSystem / LocalService / NetworkService | – | true | yes | `Manual` | Local accounts can never reach the disable path, because `ProcessDdAgentUserCredentials` generates a random 128-character password when none is supplied (`ProcessUserCustomActions.cs`), and gMSA plus the well-known accounts are already covered by `IsServiceAccount`. `IsDomainAccount` is only evaluated once the password is known to be missing, so **the common install path is unchanged**. ### Motivation Fixes IR-59268 (SEV-3). `dd-procmgr-service` moved from `LocalSystem` to `ddagentuser` in 7.82.0 and, unlike the earlier services that hit this same class of bug (security-agent, DDOT, PAR), it **runs by default**. On a manual MSI upgrade that does not re-provide `DDAGENTUSER_PASSWORD` and has no LSA secret — the case for hosts first installed with **7.65 or earlier**, since only 7.66+ began storing it: 1. `InstallServices` creates the service with a domain account and an **empty password**. 2. `ConfigureServiceUsers` sees no password and passes `null` to `SetCredentials`, which leaves the empty password in place. 3. The service fails to log on (Event 7000/7038, Security 4625 substatus `0xC000006A`). 4. Failure actions are `restart` ×3 with `RestartServiceDelayInSeconds = 60`, but **`ResetPeriodInDays = 0`** makes the SCM reset the failure counter immediately, so it applies the *first* action forever and never exhausts the three restarts. Hence Event 7031 reporting *"It has done this 1 time(s)"* on every iteration, and an **unbounded 60-second retry loop**. 5. Five failed logons **lock out the account in about 4 minutes**, unattended, on a single host — and because it is a domain account, the Agent then fails to start on **every host sharing it**. Three customers have reported it; one is uninstalling the Agent from their Windows fleet. Affected hosts already on 7.82.0–7.82.2 self-heal on upgrade, though the account still has to be unlocked once. ### Describe how you validated your changes **Unit tests** — new `CustomActions.Tests/Service/ProcmgrStartTypeTests.cs`, 8 cases: domain-without-password → `Disabled`; domain-with-password, **local-without-password**, gMSA and LocalSystem → `Manual`; `ERROR_SERVICE_DOES_NOT_EXIST` swallowed; any other failure propagates; and no other service's start type is touched. **E2E, domain** — new `testUpgradeWithoutStoredPasswordSuite` in `tests/windows/domain-test` installs **7.65.2-1** with a domain account and password, upgrades **without** a password, then asserts: - `dd-procmgr-service` start type is `SERVICE_DISABLED` - the account never appears in `Search-ADAccount -LockedOut` over a 6-minute window (the real lockout took ~4) - no System 7000/7031/7038 or Security 4625 events mentioning the service or user in that window - the core Agent is healthy and payloads reach the fakeintake - **positive control:** re-installing *with* the password restores `SERVICE_DEMAND_START` and the service starts The existing `testUpgradeSuite` does not catch this, because it installs last stable (7.82.x), which already stores the LSA secret. **E2E, non-domain** — one assertion added to `install-test`'s `TestUpgrade`, which is the exact local-account analogue (default local `ddagentuser`, upgraded without a password), asserting the service **stays enabled**. Verified locally: `7.65.2-1` is present for `x86_64` in the live `installers_v2.json`; both E2E packages pass `gofmt` and `go vet`; release note passes `linter.rst-releasenotes` and `linter.releasenote-unique-ids`. **Not yet validated — please note before reviewing:** - The C# is **not compile-verified locally** (no `dotnet`/`msbuild`/`mono` available; the projects target .NET Framework 4.6.2/4.7.2). CI's Windows MSI jobs are the first real build. - Manual QA of the reproduction from the incident is still to be done. - No existing test pins a 7.65 install, so the 7.65 → current upgrade on a domain controller may need a CI run to shake out. ### Additional Notes **Why the MSI and not `pkg/fleet/installer`** (per `.claude/rules/msi.md`): the affected path is specifically the manual MSI upgrade — fleet upgrades are unaffected. The bad credential is written by the WiX `ServiceInstall` element itself, and the fix must land between `InstallServices` and `StartDDServices` inside the same MSI transaction. `pkg/fleet/installer` is not in this code path. **Why disabling is safe:** every service uses `StartOn = null` / `StopOn = null`, `ConfigureServices` runs `When.After Step.InstallServices`, and `StartDDServices` runs later — so the service is disabled *before any logon attempt exists*. A disabled procmgr does not break the core Agent: `startDependentServices` only logs a warning when a dependent service fails to start. **Reverting is automatic.** `MajorUpgrade.Schedule = afterInstallInitialize` means every upgrade removes and recreates the services with `Start = demand`, so a disabled start type cannot persist. No registry flag or persistent state is needed. The has-password branch sets `Manual` explicitly anyway, so the outcome is deterministic rather than dependent on that sequencing. **Behavior change to be aware of:** while procmgr is disabled, DDOT / PAR / ADP do not run. Those hosts could not have run them anyway, since they need the same unavailable password. This is called out in the release note. **`ConfigureServiceUsers` went `private` → `internal`** so the tests can call it. `CustomActions/Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs` already declares `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("CustomActions.Tests")]` for exactly this, and `ConfigureUserCustomActions` already uses the same pattern. This does **not** widen the MSI's public surface. Testing through the public `ConfigureServices(Session)` is not viable: the test setup passes `rollbackDataName: null`, so the `finally { _rollbackDataStore.Store(); }` would NRE. **Rollback record deliberately omitted:** services are recreated on every upgrade, procmgr is created fresh in this transaction, and if an upgrade rolls back, leaving procmgr disabled is better than restoring a broken enabled-with-no-password config. **Not in this PR, follow-ups:** 1. **`ResetPeriodInDays = 0` is the actual reason a failed logon becomes a lockout.** It affects every dependent service. Setting it to `1` (or making the third action `none`) would bound any future crash-loop to 3 attempts. Small change, but it alters recovery behavior for all services, so it wants its own PR and QA. 2. Generic empty-password guard for all services, so the next new service can't repeat this. 3. Installer telemetry — the incident had no way to find other affected customers. 4. An `agent status` warning when procmgr is disabled for this reason. 5. #54735 / #54731 run procmgr as LocalSystem with spawn profiles, removing the ddagentuser logon entirely. Not backportable now; this MSI workaround can be relaxed once they land. Intended for backport to `7.82.x` for 7.82.3. Every production file touched is byte-identical between `main` and `origin/7.82.x`, so the cherry-pick should be conflict-free.

signal.title: healthplatform: correct the docker permission issue impact
signal.text: The check that raises this issue detects an unreachable Docker socket, so the Agent cannot query the daemon at all and container metrics, container image collection and container image vulnerability scanning all go quiet. The impact named only the log tailing fallback, so an operator chasing missing images would read the issue and dismiss it. Worse, that fallback cannot happen. Socket tailing needs the very socket that is unreachable. Everything named is scoped to Docker. The check only proves that a default Docker socket exists and cannot be opened, not that Docker is the runtime in use, so a containerd or CRI-O node with a stale inaccessible socket keeps reporting all of it through its own collector. Only the impact text changes. Title, Description and the remediation still describe the log directory case that the logs producer raised before 058e777637d removed it, and the remediation ACLs "<socket>/containers", which helps nobody whose dd-agent user is not in the docker group. Correcting that means replacing the embedded scripts, so it is left for a separate change.
signal.author: 0intro

signal.title: sbom: warn when container image scanning has no container runtime
signal.text: Container image SBOMs come from images that workloadmeta discovers through the container runtime. With no runtime the collectors stay disabled, no image entity is ever created, and the check reports itself healthy while emitting only the host SBOM. A customer spent a week on a correct configuration because nothing said the images were never found. Warn once at configuration time. The gate is sbom.container_image.enabled, which defaults to false, rather than container_image.enabled, which defaults to true and would warn on nearly every host without containers. The check is only scheduled when sbom.enabled is true, so setting sbom.container_image.enabled on its own stays as silent as before. Only Docker, containerd and CRI-O build image SBOMs, so the runtime test names those three rather than calling IsAnyContainerFeaturePresent. That helper also answers true for Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Foundry and Podman, and a Kubernetes node whose runtime socket is not mounted is precisely the case this warning exists for.
signal.author: 0intro

signal.title: env: warn when a container socket exists but is not reachable
signal.text: Feature detection reports this with log.Infof, but it runs while the configuration is still loading, so the message is buffered and only filtered against the final log level once the logger is installed. On an Agent running at log_level warn it is discarded and never written anywhere. The condition deserves a warning. On Unix socket.IsAvailable calls a socket unreachable only when the dial fails with a permission error, so the Agent user cannot open it and container metrics, container image collection and container image vulnerability scanning are all silently disabled. Windows also counts a pipe that is merely busy, but a pipe the Agent cannot open in half a second is worth surfacing too. No test. A socket that exists and cannot be opened is not something a test can build while running as root, which is how CI runs.

The rule that triggers new-e2e-sbom lists the system-probe resolver and the test tree but not the collector, so a change confined to it reaches the suite only if someone starts the job by hand. Add the collector to the rule.

signal.title: sbom: key the runtime enrichment dedup on bom-ref
signal.text: The core-agent enrichment merge rebuilds the component list of the image SBOM it annotates, dropping any component whose name and normalised version it has already emitted. That treats a name and a version as an identity, and they are not one: Trivy reports one component per install location, so a library version pinned by two lockfiles appears once per lockfile, with a bom-ref of its own for each. The merge kept the first and dropped the rest, so the payload lost real components, and the dependency graph, which the merge carries over untouched, went on referencing the ones that were gone. Deduplicate on the bom-ref instead, which is what identifies a component in CycloneDX, and emit every component that has none, since folding those together on any other key is the same mistake. The guard is still worth keeping: it was added against a stored SBOM holding one component twice, and a byte-for-byte duplicate shares its bom-ref, so that case still collapses. Duplicate name and version pairs come from the language ecosystems, so this only shows up when sbom.container_image.analyzers includes "languages".
signal.author: 0intro

signal.title: sbom: default runtime usage properties only on OS packages
signal.text: The core-agent enrichment merge walks every component of an image SBOM and copies the runtime usage properties onto the ones the system-probe report covers, then defaults LastSeenRunning to "0" and HasSetSuidBit and RunningAsRoot to "false" on all the rest. The runtime scanner reads the dpkg, rpm and apk databases only, so a language package, the image's operating-system component and Trivy's per-lockfile application components can never be reported. They were being defaulted all the same, which states that the component was watched and never seen running when in truth it was never in scope. Default the three properties only for a component the report carried or whose purl marks it an OS package. Everything else keeps them absent, which is what a consumer needs in order to tell "watched, not in use" from "unknown". Trivy maps every OS family to the deb, rpm and apk purl types, so the prefix is enough to decide, and the same three prefixes already serve this purpose in the SBOM e2e tests. Language packages only appear when sbom.container_image.analyzers includes "languages", but the operating-system component is in every image SBOM, so the new e2e phase is exercised on every enriched image the fake intake holds.
signal.author: 0intro

signal.title: compliance/k8sconfig: do not report an unreadable file as empty
signal.text: The loader stats a configuration file, reads it, then parses whatever it got. A read that fails, typically a permission denied on a kubeconfig the Agent does not own, was recorded in the errors list and otherwise ignored. Parsing no bytes at all yields an empty configuration, which is indistinguishable from a file that is really empty, and nothing downstream consults the errors list. So an unreadable file quietly became a file holding nothing. detectManagedEnvironment falls back to the kubelet kubeconfig to recognize an EKS, GKE or AKS control plane when the node labels say nothing, and it walked the three empty maps of a manufactured kubeconfig to conclude that the node was unmanaged. Content that could not be read is now left out rather than parsed, so the detection is left with nothing to go on instead of invented evidence. It still reports such a node as unmanaged, because there is no resource type for a node we cannot identify, which is a separate matter. The ownership and permissions we did manage to stat are kept, which also fixes the benchmarks looking at them. They used to see a mode of zero for an unreadable kubelet configuration file and pass. Updates CSPDE-1519.
signal.author: 0intro

signal.title: compliance/k8sconfig: fix kubelet defaults when --config is used
signal.text: Kubernetes keeps the historical command line default of a few kubelet flags to preserve the command line API, and drops them as soon as the kubelet is started with --config. The configuration file is then loaded with the KubeletConfiguration defaults instead, and only the flags that appear on the command line are applied on top of it. The loader applied the command line defaults in both cases. The two sets of defaults disagree on exactly the three settings the CIS Kubernetes benchmarks care about. A kubelet reading a configuration file that leaves them out runs with the read-only port disabled, anonymous authentication disabled and Webhook authorization, while the loader reported a read-only port on 10255, anonymous authentication enabled and an AlwaysAllow authorization mode. Neither OpenShift nor kubeadm write readOnlyPort into their rendered configuration, so their nodes failed "The kubelet read-only port should be disabled" with the port closed. The generator now carries the configuration file default next to the command line one for those three flags, and the loader picks between them depending on whether the component reads a configuration file at all. The payload version is bumped so that rules can tell the two apart. Updates CSPDE-1519.

signal.title: feat(serverless-init): add standalone MicroVM lifecycle HTTP server
signal.text: ## Summary This adds the MicroVM lifecycle HTTP server itself: an `http.Server` listening on the configured port, handling the six lifecycle hooks the AWS MicroVM platform sends — `/ready`, `/validate`, `/run`, `/resume`, `/suspend`, and `/terminate` — in **standalone** mode, i.e. the agent answers each hook itself rather than forwarding it to a user application (that pass-through mode is added later in this stack). The motivation is to give the agent visibility into a MicroVM's full lifecycle without requiring any cooperation from the user's own application: `/ready` reports child-process liveness so the platform knows when it's safe to snapshot; `/run`/`/resume`/`/suspend`/`/terminate` each emit an enhanced lifecycle metric (tagged with the MicroVM instance ID once known), and `/suspend`/`/terminate` additionally flush all pending telemetry (metrics, traces, logs) before responding, since those are the two points where telemetry could otherwise be lost — either frozen into a snapshot or torn down with the VM. `/run`'s request body (the `runHookPayload` a caller passes to `RunMicrovm`) is capped at **1 MiB** via `http.MaxBytesReader` before being buffered; a body exceeding the cap, or any other read error, aborts the handler with a 500 rather than silently forwarding a truncated body. This cap is a self-imposed defensive bound, not a value taken from an AWS-published limit — the AWS Lambda MicroVM reference docs describe `runHookPayload` only qualitatively (tenant IDs, signed URLs, secret references) and state no numeric size limit. ## Stack This is **PR 2 of 4** in a split of https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/53035 ("feat(serverless-init): add MicroVM lifecycle HTTP server and env-var wiring"), which was too large to review as a single PR. The full stack, in merge order: 1. wire MicroVM lifecycle server config from env vars 2. **(this PR)** add standalone MicroVM lifecycle HTTP server 3. propagate MicroVM ID to logs and trace tags 4. add MicroVM lifecycle user-app forwarder pass-through The tip of PR 4 is byte-for-byte identical to the original `tianning.li/microvm-06-lifecycle-server-wire` branch. Note: this PR is somewhat larger than the ~300-line target used elsewhere in the stack — the server skeleton (types, `NewServer`, all six handlers, the shared flush path) is a single cohesive, self-contained unit and its test suite cannot be meaningfully subdivided without breaking that self-containment. ## Test plan ``` bazel test //cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle:lifecycle_test ``` - [x] `bazel build //cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle:lifecycle` - [x] `bazel test //cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle:lifecycle_test` - [x] `dda inv linter.go --targets=./cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle` 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: [SBOM] Skip images whose SBOM cannot be uncompressed
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? processImageSBOM logged the error from UncompressSBOM and carried on, but UncompressSBOM returns no SBOM alongside its error, so reading its status a few lines later dereferenced a nil pointer. The check worker recovers from a panic in Run, so that one misbehaving check cannot take the process with it, but the long-running check wrapper returns from Run as soon as it has started the goroutine the check really runs on, and the recover never covers that goroutine. An image whose stored SBOM cannot be uncompressed therefore brings the whole Agent down, and does so again at every refresh for as long as workloadmeta holds it. Skip the image instead. It is reported again once it is scanned anew.

signal.title: [procmgr] Windows spawn profiles foundation
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Introduces **Windows spawn profiles** in dd-procmgr so managed children can run under different security contexts: - **Privileged**: spawn as LocalSystem (supervisor primary token) - **AgentUser**: spawn as the agent service account (`ddagentuser`) Adds the Windows spawn stack (token logon, user profile load, supervision job, suspended `CreateProcessAsUserW`), a **privileged spawn catalog** that rejects unexpected command/args/env for privileged children, and **gRPC named-pipe caller authentication** for mutating RPCs. Also refactors the daemon runtime into a **`Supervisor` event loop** plus `ProcessManager` handlers, and runs **dd-procmgr-service as LocalSystem** so agent-profile spawn can read the agent password from LSA. **Stack context (PR 1):** | # | PR | Notes | |---|-----|--------| | 1 | This PR | spawn profiles + LocalSystem MSI | | 2 | [#54732](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54732) | config gates | | 3 | [#54734](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54734) | secret backend | | 4 | [#54735](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54735) | process-agent dual-mode | | 5 | [#53568](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/53568) | list/describe (parallel on this PR; not on the merge spine) | | 6 | [#55080](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/55080) | reload | **Explicitly deferred:** config gates (#54732), secret-backend cache invalidation (#54734), process-agent dual-mode (#54735), full `ReloadConfig` (#55080). RPC/CLI for reload stay in this PR but return `UNIMPLEMENTED` until #55080. ### Motivation Process-agent on Windows must run as LocalSystem; other agent children should stay on the agent user. Spawn profiles make that explicit and enforceable at spawn time, and are a prerequisite for moving process-agent supervision off legacy SCM in #54735. LocalSystem MSI lands here so agent-profile children (ADP, PAR, DDOT) can spawn without waiting for #54735. ### Describe how you validated your changes - Bazel/Cargo procmgr Rust unit tests (Linux + Windows CI) - Privileged spawn catalog and spawn-profile unit tests (`pkg/procmgr/rust/...`) - COAT package tests (`pkg/procmgr/coat/...`) - Windows new-e2e: ADP, PAR, DDOT running tests, plus LocalSystem / agent-user identity checks (`test/new-e2e/tests/agent-runtimes/procmgr/`) ### Additional Notes - **Fleet:** DDOT extension uninstall uses `ReloadOrRestartProcmgr()` (reload stub → SCM restart fallback). No process-agent dual-mode changes in this PR. - **ReloadConfig:** Proto and `dd-procmgr reload` remain for API compatibility; handler returns `UNIMPLEMENTED` until [#55080](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/55080). - Supersedes the spawn portion of [#53249](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/53249).

signal.title: [7.82.x] ci(ddot): make otel apt mirror resilient to slow mirrors
signal.text: Backport of #55108 to `7.82.x`. ### What does this PR do? Makes the apt package-mirror config in `Dockerfiles/agent-ddot/Dockerfile.agent-otel` (used by `docker_image_build_otel`) resilient to *slow* mirrors: - Adds `Acquire::Retries` + a 15s `Acquire` timeout so a stalled request is dropped and retried against the next mirror. - Lists mirrors as peers (drops the `priority:1` pin) and adds `us-west-2` and `mirror.leaseweb.net`, so apt load-balances and fails over across them. ### Motivation `docker_image_build_otel` intermittently timed out (~3% of runs). The full 30-40m was spent in `apt-get install build-essential` against a congested `us-east-1` mirror; the old `priority:1` pin only failed over when that mirror was fully unreachable, not when merely slow. ### Describe how you validated your changes Clean cherry-pick of the `main` commit. CI will exercise the real build here. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: [WP] Read OTel thread local context records (OTEP 4947)
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds support for reading span/trace IDs from native applications using the OpenTelemetry Thread Local Context Record format (OTel spec #4947) in the CWS eBPF security module. The implementation adds a new eBPF read path that: Discovers the OTel TLSDESC TLS variable offset (registered by user-space) Dereferences the TLS pointer to locate the OTel Thread Local Context Record This targets native applications using ELF TLSDESC (C, C++, Rust, Java/JNI, .NET/FFI, Python native extensions). ### Motivation The OpenTelemetry specification defines a standard mechanism for SDKs to publish thread-level trace context (trace ID, span ID) through ELF Thread Local Storage so that out-of-process readers like eBPF probes can correlate security events with distributed traces. Supporting this standard allows CWS to automatically pick up span context from any OTel-instrumented native application without requiring Datadog-specific instrumentation. ### Describe how you validated your changes * All modified Go packages (probe/erpc, probe/constantfetch, ebpf/probes, ptracer, probe) build cleanly * The C syscall tester compiles successfully with the new otel-span-open command * Added a functional test (TestOTelSpan) that: * Creates a __thread TLS variable in C, computes its offset from fsbase via arch_prctl(ARCH_GET_FS) * Registers the offset with eBPF via the new REGISTER_OTEL_TLS_OP eRPC operation * Fills an OTel Thread Local Context Record with a known trace ID and span ID in W3C byte order * Triggers an open() syscall and verifies the correct trace/span IDs appear in the captured security event ### Additional Notes

signal.title: [procmgr] Show profile and user in list and describe
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Expose spawn identity in the process manager API and `dd-procmgr` CLI: - `list`: adds `profile` and `user` columns (table + JSON) - `describe`: adds `Profile`, `User`, and `Runtime User` (only when the process is running and lookup succeeds) Proto changes: - `Process`: `profile`, `user` - `ProcessDetail`: `profile`, `user`, `runtime_user` Implementation notes: - `profile` is derived from the process name (`agent` / `privileged`) - `user` is the intended / last-spawn account, stored on `ManagedProcess` and refreshed on spawn - `runtime_user` is resolved from the OS at describe time (Windows token owner / Linux `/proc` + `getpwuid`) - Windows display formatting is centralized in `AccountName` **Stack context:** Parallel on [#54731](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54731). Nothing else in the stack depends on this PR. | # | PR | Notes | |---|-----|--------| | 1 | [#54731](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54731) | spawn profiles + LocalSystem MSI | | 2 | [#54732](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54732) | config gates | | 3 | [#54734](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54734) | secret backend | | 4 | [#54735](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/54735) | process-agent dual-mode | | 5 | This PR | list/describe (parallel on spawn profiles) | | 6 | [#55080](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/55080) | reload | ### Motivation After Windows spawn profiles land, operators need a simple way to see how each managed child is spawned without reading code or registry state. Showing `profile` and `user` in `list`/`describe` makes SCM migration behavior visible (e.g. process-agent as `privileged` / `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` vs other children as `agent` / installer user). `runtime_user` in `describe` helps debug cases where the running PID differs from the intended spawn account. ### Describe how you validated your changes - `cargo test --lib --bin dd-procmgr` (procmgr Rust unit tests) - `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/procmgr/coat/...` - Updated procmgr CLI e2e tests for `profile` / `user` / `runtime_user` output ### Additional Notes - `user` reflects spawn policy (intended or last used), not a live registry re-read on every query - `runtime_user` is omitted from `list` and from `describe` when PID is unset or lookup fails (debug log only) - No COAT/metrics changes in this PR

signal.title: Enables the v3 metrics intake for series in DDOT
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Enables the **v3 metrics intake for series** in DDOT (the `otel-agent` binary). ### Motivation OTAGENT-1130, under epic OTAGENT-1133 ("Reduce customer metrics egress bandwidth 30–50% with v3 payload"). DDOT was the last OTel surface still on the v2 series intake. This PR moves DDOT onto the v3 series path, aligning it with the core Agent (series v3 default since 7.81). ### Describe how you validated your changes - **Unit:** `cmd/otel-agent/config` tests pass; the guard tests now assert the resolved value is `datadog_only`. - **Static:** `dda inv linter.go` — 0 issues; `dda inv otel-agent.build` — OK. - **Manual (local, standalone otel-agent → fakeintake, `DD_USE_V3_API_SERIES_ENABLED=true`, zstd):** series routed to `/api/intake/metrics/v3/series` and **0** on `/api/v2/series`; all payloads zstd (wire magic `28b52ffd`); v3 payloads decode correctly; a cumulative Sum arrived as a delta `COUNT` (c2d); sketches stayed on `/api/beta/sketches` (v2). - **Manual + telemetrygen + delta** - metrics are posted to https://api.datadoghq.com/api/intake/metrics/v3/series" (202 Accepted) - **Manual + telemetrygen + cumulative** - metrics are converted to delta & posted to https://api.datadoghq.com/api/intake/metrics/v3/series" (202 Accepted) - **E2E:** new `TestOTelAgentV3Series` (KinD DDOT with v3 enabled) asserts OTLP metrics reach the intake, series land on the v3 endpoint (`RouteStats`), and v3 payloads are zstd. Auto-wired into the `new-e2e-otel` job — no CI changes. (Runs in CI on this PR.) ### Additional Notes - **Kill-switch / rollout:** enablement follows `use_v3_api.series.enabled` (default `datadog_only`). v2 remains the compat/fallback path (non-Datadog destinations, non-zstd builds, non-migrated regions). Opt out with `use_v3_api.series.enabled=false` (or `DD_USE_V3_API_SERIES_ENABLED=false`). - **Scope:** series only. Sketches (distributions) stay on v2 (v3 for sketches is a separate opt-in). - **Known follow-up (this PR):** the auto-injected `datadog/dd-autoconfigured` flare extension keeps its own zlib serializer and now logs a benign but misleading "disabling v3 metrics intake" warning — the same warning #52301 suppressed on the OSS path, surfaced because v3 is now enabled in-process. Egress is unaffected (verified v3 + zstd); the warning does not reflect the actual series path. To be addressed. - this deliberately does **not** revert #52301 (`serializerexporter/serializer.go`). That line only runs for the OSS Datadog exporter in opentelemetry-collector-contrib - for case "datadog_only" - the PR updates "use_v3_api.series.endpoints" by "https://api.xxxx" https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/OTAGENT-1130

signal.title: Convert linux_bpf to linux && bpf build tags
signal.text: <!--Please give us some feedback on your experience writing this PR ! https://app.datadoghq.com/forms/43db4c02-6837-400c-8083-692e141b1b88 !--> ### What does this PR do? Bazel requires a hint to understand whether a certain package is OS specific or not. One of the ways to do that is to use platform build tags like `linux`, `windows`, etc. In our case `linux_bpf` was de facto a platform constraint, but Bazel and Gazelle, a tool we use to automatically manage BUILD files, were not aware of that, so certain Linux only libraries were becoming unconditional dependencies for all the platforms. That was leading to failed builds and test executions. So, the simplest way out of this was to rename `linux_bpf` into `bpf` and add `linux` tag everywhere to have `linux && bpf`. ### Motivation First, it is technically more correct to rely more on standard go build tags. Second, this paves us the way to get rid of `bpf` tag in the near future. ### Additional Notes **Go Package Import Differences** is a false positive. Change in build tags led to a change in baseline being pretty much empty for the new layout. There are no changes in the imports

signal.title: [SBOM] Refresh every image when spreading the refresh
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? The spread refresher divides the image count by the number of steps it spreads a period over to decide how many images to refresh per step. The division truncates, so a host with fewer than ten images refreshed none of them, ever. An image SBOM was then sent only when the image changed or when a container first ran it, so inUse stayed true after the last container stopped. Above ten, unless the count was a multiple of ten, the refresh was merely slower than configured. Fifteen images took one and a half periods to cycle. Round the count up. Every image is then covered within one period, at the cost of at most nine extra refreshes per period. That overhead only matters where images are few, and a host with a single image now sends it once per step rather than once per period. The refresher is off by default, so this only affects hosts that set sbom.container_image.use_spread_refresher.

signal.title: fix(serverless-init): eliminate GlobalTags data race in MicroVM trace tags
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Stops MicroVM's async `/run` lifecycle hook from mutating `Agent.GlobalTags` and routes the dynamic `lambda_microvm_id` tag update through the (already serverless-owned) span modifier instead. Concretely: - `pkg/serverless/trace/span_modifier.go`: `tags` field is now `atomic.Pointer[map[string]string]` (using `go.uber.org/atomic`, per repo convention); `ModifySpan` applies each tag lock-free via `Load()`. - `pkg/serverless/trace/trace.go`: adds `UpdateRuntimeTags`, which updates only the span modifier — never `GlobalTags`. The existing `SetTags` (called once, synchronously, at startup before the trace agent runs) is untouched and still updates both. - `cmd/serverless-init/main.go`: the two async `TraceTagSetterFunc` closures wired into the MicroVM lifecycle server now call `UpdateRuntimeTags` instead of `SetTags`. - `cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle/server.go`: updated a doc comment that named the (now stale) method satisfying `TraceTagSetter`. ### Motivation Codex flagged a data race on #53036: `serverlessTraceAgent.SetTags` is invoked from a goroutine inside the MicroVM lifecycle server's `/run` handler, which runs concurrently with the trace agent's span-processing loop. `SetTags` calls `Agent.SetGlobalTagsUnsafe`, whose own doc comment says "Unsafe for concurrent use" — it does a bare `a.conf.GlobalTags = tags` write, while `pkg/trace/agent/agent.go` (hot path, lines 531/711) and `pkg/trace/api/telemetry.go` read `a.conf.GlobalTags` with no synchronization at all. `GlobalTags` is computed once at config-build time, before the trace agent starts running, and every one of those readers assumes that invariant holds forever — MicroVM's dynamic per-invocation tag update is the only thing in the codebase that breaks it. In practice the write is a pointer swap to a new map rather than an in-place mutation, so the realistic worst case is a span in flight at the moment of the swap missing `lambda_microvm_id` — not a crash. But it's a genuine data race under the Go memory model: `go test -race` / `bazel test --config=race` will flag it the moment a concurrent test exercises this path, and nothing guarantees it stays benign under future compiler optimizations. The fix avoids touching any code shared with the non-serverless trace agent (`pkg/trace/agent`, `pkg/trace/api`, `pkg/trace/config`) by reusing `SpanModifier`, which already runs at the identical point in `agent.go`'s span-processing loop (right after the `GlobalTags` loop) and is exclusively serverless-owned. Its `tags` field existed before this change but was dead code — written by `SetTags`, never read by `ModifySpan`; this fix makes it real. This is scoped entirely to MicroVM. Every other cloud service (`AppService`, `CloudRun`, `ContainerApp`, `CloudRunJobs`) ignores `LifecycleCtx` in `Init`, so they never invoke the async closures — they only ever call the original, still-synchronous `SetTags` once at startup, unchanged by this PR. ### Describe how you validated your changes Added regression coverage for every change (7 new/extended tests): - `TestSpanModifierSetTagsConcurrentWithModifySpan` — hammers `SetTags`/`ModifySpan` from two goroutines under the race detector; this is the actual bug repro. - `TestSpanModifierModifySpanBeforeSetTags`, `...AppliesTagsSetDynamically`, `...ReflectsLatestSetTags` — functional coverage of the new atomic-pointer-backed tag application. - `TestServerlessTraceAgentSetTagsUpdatesGlobalTagsAndSpanModifier` — confirms the untouched synchronous `SetTags` path still updates both `GlobalTags` and the span modifier. - `TestServerlessTraceAgentUpdateRuntimeTagsDoesNotTouchGlobalTags` — the core assertion: `UpdateRuntimeTags` never writes `GlobalTags`. - `TestServerlessTraceAgentUpdateRuntimeTagsNoSpanModifier` — no-op safety when `SpanModifier` doesn't implement `taggable`. - Extended `TestSetupWithoutAPIKey` to also exercise `noopTraceAgent.UpdateRuntimeTags`. Run locally with: ```sh dda inv test --targets=./pkg/serverless/trace,./cmd/serverless-init,./cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle,./cmd/serverless-init/cloudservice --race dda inv linter.go --targets=./pkg/serverless/trace,./cmd/serverless-init,./cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle,./cmd/serverless-init/cloudservice ``` All 302 tests pass (4 skipped, platform-gated) with the race detector enabled; linter reports 0 issues. ### Additional Notes Stacked on #53096 (`tianning.li/microvm-07-05-main-wiring`) — base branch will move to `main` once that merges. `BUILD.bazel` files were checked (`bazel run //:gazelle -- update` + buildifier on the one Gazelle-managed directory touched, `cmd/serverless-init/lifecycle`); no changes needed since the rest of the touched files are under pre-existing `gazelle:exclude` directives (not yet Bazel-migrated). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: feat(softinv): report the OS and OEM kernel-mode drivers
signal.text: <!--Please give us some feedback on your experience writing this PR ! https://app.datadoghq.com/forms/43db4c02-6837-400c-8083-692e141b1b88 !--> ### What does this PR do? Extends the software inventory beyond installed applications with two new software types, `os` and `driver`: | Platform | Type | Source | |---|---|---| | Windows | `driver` | `Win32_SystemDriver`, plus `Win32_PnPSignedDriver` joined against `Win32_PnPEntity` | | Windows | `os` | `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion` | | macOS | `os` | `/System/Library/CoreServices/SystemVersion.plist` | **Operating system.** One entry whose version advances, rather than one entry per update. An update is an event, not an installed item whose version moves, so it would produce a permanently static entry — and the host SBOM already carries installed KBs. Name and product code are constant, because the backend keys an item on name + product code with the version excluded; anything version-derived in either field would make an upgrade read as remove + install. The version carries the full patch level: `10.0.26100.4652` on Windows including the UBR, `15.6 (24G84)` on macOS including the build that supplemental updates and RSRs advance. **Drivers.** Only OEM and third-party drivers are reported; the drivers that ship with Windows are excluded. Two sources, because each sees what the other cannot. `Win32_SystemDriver` covers drivers registered as kernel services, including software-only ones — EDR minifilters, network and DLP filters — that have no PnP device node. The class carries no version or vendor, so both come from the version resource of the image path; only the numeric `VS_FIXEDFILEINFO` version is accepted, since the `FileVersion` string is routinely decorated or comma-separated. Image paths are normalized (`\??\`, `\SystemRoot\`, `%SystemRoot%`, relative) and MUI display names (`@<dll>,-<id>`) resolved with `SHLoadIndirectString`. Filtered on the binary's `CompanyName`, the only vendor signal the class offers; an absent `CompanyName` is kept, since an unattributed kernel driver is worth seeing. Identity is the service name, which Windows guarantees unique. `Win32_PnPSignedDriver` covers packages bound to a device that register no kernel service of their own, which the first source cannot see. Selected by the INF being published as `oemNN.inf` — `Manufacturer` is not used, because Microsoft's inbox INFs report generic strings such as `(Standard system devices)` and Windows also ships inbox INFs authored by hardware vendors, so filtering on it would keep hundreds of inbox drivers. One `Win32_PnPEntity` query is joined in memory to skip devices that already have a service; a query per device would spend the entire time budget on the join. Identity is the device name, the field the class offers that survives a driver update. Known limitations: UMDF user-mode drivers register no kernel service, and a driver whose service entry is created, loaded, then deleted is invisible. This is an inventory of registered drivers, not of code currently in the kernel. **Deadline.** Each collector is bounded at 90s in the shared snapshot runner. A timeout is fatal, because a timed-out enumeration is an unknown state and a missing row reads downstream as a removal; zero rows is still a valid result. A hung native call cannot be cancelled — the WMI library takes no context — so a collector that misses its deadline is not started again until it returns. ### Motivation The inventory only covered installed applications, leaving OS patch level and kernel drivers invisible — two of the most useful signals for fleet visibility and compliance. The deadline is a prerequisite rather than a nicety: these sources can block, and a single slow `Collect()` previously stalled the whole snapshot with no upper bound. ### Describe how you validated your changes - Windows unit tests run and pass in CI (`tests_windows-x64`); macOS unit tests pass locally; `bazel test //pkg/inventory/software:software_test` passes. - `dda inv linter.go` clean, and clean again under `GOOS=windows`, which type-checks the Windows-tagged files and their tests. - Coverage: deadline and in-flight behaviour, both driver filters, the PnP/service join including case mismatch and devices missing from `Win32_PnPEntity`, path normalization and MUI resolution, the numeric-version requirement, identity stability across a version bump for both driver sources, and entry-ID uniqueness once the new families merge with application entries. - Real-host integration tests compare collected drivers against the `Services` registry key, assert nothing Microsoft-published survives the service filter, and log the OEM/inbox split per source; the macOS one asserts the running version against `sw_vers -productVersion`. - Driver payloads from a real Windows host were inspected end to end. That caught two drivers reporting an unresolved MUI reference as their name, fixed in 2741b66. ### Additional Notes - A fatal error from any single collector still drops the whole snapshot (existing behaviour). - PnP-sourced entries carry no `install_paths`, because `Win32_PnPSignedDriver` names no binary. - Enable with `software_inventory.enabled: true`, which drives both the system-probe module and the core agent component. No status or flare changes were needed, since `populateStatus` already groups by `Source`. - Worst-case snapshot duration is bounded per collector, not globally, so it scales with collector count. A snapshot-wide ceiling would be a separate change.

signal.title: fix(e2e): Avoid secret propagation to copy file paths
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Removes secret propagation from the temporary pathname generated by `CopyInlineFile` while preserving secrecy on the inline file contents. This prevents the pathname from tainting the `CopyFile` triggers array as secret and allows Pulumi to serialize the remote copy resource during previews. ### Motivation Inline Agent configuration includes secret values such as the API key. Because the temporary pathname is produced by an `ApplyT` on that content, Pulumi marks the pathname secret even though it contains no file contents. Passing that secret pathname through the remote copy triggers caused previews to fail with `malformed RPC secret: missing value for "triggers"`. ### Describe how you validated your changes - Ran `dda inv test --module=./test/e2e-framework --targets=./components/command/...`. - Reproduced the preview failure with both Pulumi CLI 3.257.0 and 3.253.0 before the change. - Ran `dda inv aws.create-vm --use-fakeintake` after the change. Pulumi preview completed and the update successfully created all 29 resources, including the EC2 host, healthy fakeintake ECS service, and running Agent.

signal.title: Reduce metric filtering overhead
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Reduces the cost of Observer metric filtering by checking source names before copying and sorting tags (if processing rules don't have tags). ### Why? From staging profiles, unnecessary metrics filtering allocations was one of the biggest consumers of observer CPU. ### Results Representative local benchmarks using the V1 allowlist and a high-tag metric sample: | Path | Before | After | |---|---:|---:| | Rejected metric | ~437 ns/op, 256 B/op, 1 alloc/op | ~78 ns/op, 0 B/op, 0 allocs/op | | Metric accepted by the first rule | ~333 ns/op, 320 B/op, 2 allocs/op | ~337 ns/op, 320 B/op, 2 allocs/op | | Metric accepted by the last rule | ~456 ns/op, 320 B/op, 2 allocs/op | ~392 ns/op, 320 B/op, 2 allocs/op | | Parallel rejected handle path | ~222 ns/op, 16 B/op, 1 alloc/op | ~104 ns/op, 0 B/op, 0 allocs/op |
