signal.title: feat(serverless-init): add shared infrastructure for AWS MicroVM cloud service
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds the shared Go infrastructure that AWS MicroVM cloud-service support depends on. This is the first in a stack of PRs that together deliver full MicroVM observability. ### Motivation The Datadog Agent's serverless-init supports multiple cloud platforms (Cloud Run, Container Apps, etc.) via a `CloudService` abstraction. AWS Lambda MicroVMs are a new deployment target where the Agent runs as an init process inside a Firecracker microVM. Each new platform requires small additions in a few central places before the platform-specific code can be wired in cleanly. This PR makes those additions in isolation so the platform-specific MicroVM PR is a clean diff: - **`pkg/metrics/metricsource.go`** — adds `MetricSourceAWSMicroVMEnhanced`, the metric source tag used on all MicroVM enhanced metrics. - **`pkg/serverless/env/env.go`** — adds `MicroVMImageARNEnvVar` (`AWS_LAMBDA_MICROVM_IMAGE_ARN`), the env var the platform injects with the image ARN. - **`pkg/serializer/internal/metrics/origin_mapping.go`** — maps the new MetricSource to its origin string so metrics are routed correctly in the serializer. - **`comp/dogstatsd/server/impl/default_serverless.go` + `enrich.go`** — threads MicroVM origin/tag enrichment through DogStatsD's serverless path. - **`comp/logs-library/processor/json_serverless_init.go`** — adds a JSON log encoder for structured serverless-init logs, needed for MicroVM's log pipeline. ### Describe how you validated your changes - New unit tests cover the origin mapping and DogStatsD enrichment paths. - All changes are additive; no existing behaviour is altered. Run the unit tests for the packages touched by this PR: ``` dda inv test --targets=./comp/dogstatsd/server/impl,./comp/logs-library/processor,./pkg/metrics,./pkg/serializer/internal/metrics,./pkg/serverless/env ``` ### Additional Notes **PR stack** (each PR bases on the one above): 1. **This PR** — shared infrastructure 2. `microvm-02-cloudservice-run` — `Run()` method on `CloudService` interface 3. `microvm-03-lifecycle-config-childhandle` — lifecycle package primitives 4. `microvm-04-lifecycle-forwarder` — HTTP pass-through proxy 5. `microvm-05-lifecycle-heartbeat` — periodic heartbeat metric 6. `microvm-06-lifecycle-server-wire` — lifecycle HTTP server 7. `microvm-07-microvm-service-wiring` — MicroVM `CloudService` + main wiring 8. `microvm-08-sigusr2-on-run` — SIGUSR2 on `/run` for PRNG reseeding

signal.text: ### What Swap the CWS legacy proprietary TLS APM-correlation path for a Go pprof-label span-context reader, on top of the thread-context groundwork. - **Remove legacy TLS**: `fill_span_context_legacy`, the `span_tls` map/struct, its eRPC registration, and the ebpfless ptracer span reader. `fill_span_context` is kept as the dispatch stub. - **Add tail-calls after hooks**: fill_span_context is growing and is inlined in almost every hook. Setup tail-calls after as many hooks to avoid this blowup. - **Add Go pprof reader** (`span_go.h`, `go_labels.go`): reads dd-trace-go's goroutine pprof labels by walking TLS → runtime.g → runtime.m → curg → labels, using per-process offsets resolved from the Go binary. Labels are parsed lazily in userspace to both reduce code blowup and processing time in eBPF. - **Misc**: tolerate a missing login UID (ENOENT); drive the procfs resolver test with a spawned child. ### Testing Functional tests `TestGoSpan` and `TestDDTraceGoSpan` pass.

signal.title: fix(serverless-init): prevent stale log tag cache prime from clobbering /run update
signal.text: ## Summary - Background: `cachedTags` is an `atomic.Pointer[string]` (not a plain `string`, as on `main` before serverless-init supported MicroVM) because MicroVM's `/run` lifecycle hook can call `SetServerlessInitTagCache` from the HTTP lifecycle-hook server goroutine concurrently with `Encode` running on the log-processing goroutine. A plain string would risk a torn read (mismatched pointer/length) under that concurrent access; the atomic pointer keeps the hot path lock-free while making updates race-free. - Restores `CompareAndSwap(nil, &s)` (as `jsonServerlessInitEncoder.primeTagsFromMessage`) for `Encode`'s cold-path cache prime, replacing the plain `Store()` that PR #53030 landed in response to review comment [r3530721641](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pull/53030/discussion_r3530721641). - That comment's reasoning ("all callers compute the same tags anyway") only covers `Encode` racing `Encode`. It doesn't cover `Encode` racing `SetServerlessInitTagCache` — a second writer, driven by the MicroVM `/run` hook, that pushes an authoritative, possibly newer tag set into the same field. With a plain `Store`, a stale cold-path write computed before that update can land after it and silently clobber the correct value, reverting subsequent log tags to the pre-launch set. - Only MicroVM exercises this second writer today (verified: `AppService`/`CloudRun`/`ContainerApp`/`LocalService.Init` discard `*TracingContext`; `CloudRunJobs.Init` never reads `.LifecycleCtx`; only `MicroVM.Init` wires `LogsTagSetter` through to `SetServerlessInitTagCache`), so Cloud Run / Azure Container Apps / local mode are unaffected either way. ## Test plan - [x] Added `TestJSONServerlessInitEncoder_ColdPathPrimeNeverClobbersConcurrentUpdate`, which sequences the race deterministically (no goroutines) and asserts the authoritative value survives. - [x] Verified the new test fails against a plain-`Store()` version of `primeTagsFromMessage` and passes against the CAS version. - [x] `dda inv test --targets=./comp/logs-library/processor/...` (with and without `--race`) — all 43 tests pass. - [x] `dda inv linter.go --targets=./comp/logs-library/processor/...` — 0 issues. - [x] `bazel run //:gazelle -- ./comp/logs-library/processor` — no `BUILD.bazel` changes needed (no new files/deps). - [x] `bazel build`/`bazel test //comp/logs-library/processor:...` — pass. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: ci: make apt mirror config resilient to slow mirrors across agent images
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Makes CI Docker builds resilient to slow public package mirrors, across every image in this repo that installs packages from a public host — each fitted to its own package system. **Ubuntu (apt) — multi-URI failover** (`agent`, `base-image`, `cluster-agent`, `otel-agent`, `ddot-ebpf`, podman e2e resource): apt's `mirror` method can't fail over off a *slow* mirror (only a fully-unreachable one), so instead of a mirrorlist we rewrite the deb822 `URIs:` fields in `ubuntu.sources` to an ordered multi-URI list. apt tries them in order and fails over on error. Drop `us-east-1` (chronically slow in every timeout log); order `us-west-2` → `archive.ubuntu.com` → `mirror.leaseweb.net`. `Retries "1"` + 10s timeout so a slow mirror becomes a fast error. **Debian (apt)** (`test/fakeintake`, golang base): rewrite `debian.sources` `URIs:` to Debian's AWS/CloudFront mirror `cdn-aws.deb.debian.org` first, `deb.debian.org` fallback, + Acquire timeout/Retries. (Debian has no EC2 archive mirror like Ubuntu; cdn-aws is its AWS-region CDN.) **Alpine (apk)** (`Dockerfiles/dogstatsd/alpine`, `test/fakeintake` deploy stage): list `dl-cdn` primary + `mirror.clarkson.edu` secondary (apk fails over in listed order), and add the global `apk --timeout` so a slow mirror fails fast. ### Motivation `docker_build_host_profiler_standalone_amd64` was timing out (~30m, across many branches incl. 7.83.x). Its `release` stage builds on `agent-base-image` (= `Dockerfiles/agent/Dockerfile`), whose `apt-get` stalled against a congested `us-east-1`. An earlier attempt (mirror+file peer list + Acquire timeout) did **not** stop it: job `1965243524` showed apt sticking to the slow `us-east-1` and retrying the same URI to the job timeout, even though `us-west-2` served ~90 packages in one second when apt picked it. The `mirror` method has no per-request failover on slowness — hence the switch to explicit ordered `URIs:`. ### Describe how you validated your changes - CI Visibility + job logs pinpointed the stall inside the apt step of the agent-base-image release stage on a slow `us-east-1`, and showed `us-west-2` healthy. - Validated the Ubuntu and Debian `sed` `URIs:` rewrites against the default noble `ubuntu.sources` / trixie `debian.sources` (GNU sed semantics). - Confirmed `apk --timeout` is a valid global flag (must precede the subcommand). - CI will exercise the real builds here. ### Additional Notes Local dev-tooling Dockerfiles (`tools/gdb`, `tools/ebpf/*-agent-dev`) are excluded — they don't run under `CI=true` and aren't in any CI build path. `agent-ddot/Dockerfile.agent-otel` is handled by #55108. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: [NETPATH-1108] Remove flaky RC re-poll gate from Dynamic Path e2e test Setup
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Fixes the synchronization in `TestHostTrafficDynamicPathSuite` without relying on fakeintake's global Remote Config poll counter. - Adds the `NETWORK_PATH` Remote Config document immediately after `BaseSuite.SetupSuite`, before curl, DNS, and resolver setup. - Removes both `RCStats().Polls` gates. - Keeps the traffic generator running for 6 minutes so it outlives the test's 5-minute eventual assertion. JIRA: [NETPATH-1108](https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/NETPATH-1108) ### Motivation The suite has intermittently failed on `main` in `SetupSuite` with: > `agent did not poll Remote Config after the dynamic config was added` The E2E framework configures the Agent to poll fakeintake every 5 seconds, so the production default 1-minute cadence was not the cause. The flake came from the interaction between the test's setup order and fakeintake's empty Remote Config behavior: 1. The suite performed package, DNS, and resolver setup before adding its first `NETWORK_PATH` config. 2. During that time, the Agent polled fakeintake's empty RC repository. 3. Fakeintake records those requests in `RCStats().Polls` but returns HTTP 404 when no requested product has a config. 4. Those responses increased the Agent's exponential retry backoff, so the next poll could fall outside the setup gate's 2-minute deadline. The poll counter was also not a reliable synchronization signal: it increments before fakeintake knows whether the request can be served and therefore does not prove that this config was fetched or applied. Taking the counter baseline after `RCAddConfig` also allowed a successful fetch between those two calls to be missed, forcing the test to wait for an unnecessary additional poll. The test's existing payload assertion is the stronger end-to-end proof. Local configuration excludes all destinations, and the expected Network Path event must contain the exact remote `test_config_id`, `test_config_source`, and tags. Observing that event proves the config was fetched, applied by the deployed Agent, exercised by matching host traffic, and forwarded to fakeintake. Adding the config first minimizes empty-repository polling during setup. Keeping traffic active beyond the full assertion window ensures a delayed RC application still receives matching connections to admit. ### Describe how you validated your changes - `git diff --check` - Confirmed the existing `new-e2e-netpath` CI job covers `./tests/netpath`. - Local live E2E was intentionally skipped; `new-e2e-netpath` will exercise the change in CI. No production code is changed. [NETPATH-1108]: https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/NETPATH-1108?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNWRkNTljNzYxNjVmNDY3MDlhMDU5Y2ZhYzA5YTRkZjUiLCJwIjoiZ2l0aHViLWNvbS1KU1cifQ

signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Fix format-string bugs in `pkg/trace` and add `github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/pkg/trace/log` to the govet `printf` `funcs` allowlist in `.golangci.yml` so this class of bug is caught by CI going forward. ### Motivation pkg/trace logger has printf style commands but the govet rule didn't know about this so there were a few spots where the printf directives were wrong ### Describe how you validated your changes - `dda inv linter.go --module=pkg/trace` → `0 issues.` / `All linters passed` (after all fixes; before the fixes it reported the 5 originally-known findings plus 2 additional `%s`-with-non-Stringer findings, all now fixed). - `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/trace/agent,./pkg/trace/filters` → all tests pass (403 tests, 3 pre-existing skips unrelated to this change). - `git diff origin/main` reviewed line-by-line to confirm the legacy `*pb.Span` code paths (`normalize`, `Truncate`) were left untouched — on `pb.Span`, `Resource`/`Name` are struct fields and the existing `s.Resource`/`s.Name` usages there are correct as-is. - `dda inv linter.go --targets=./cmd/serverless-init,./comp/core/log/impl-trace,./comp/process/gpusubscriber/impl,./pkg/config/remote/uptane,./pkg/privateactionrunner/bundles/helm,./cmd/process-agent/subcommands/status` → `0 issues.` (sanity check that no other consumer of `pkg/trace/log` regressed). - Added a `fixes:` release note via `reno new trace-log-printf-format-fixes`. ### Additional Notes ### Why not `DebugString()` `*idx.InternalSpan` does have a `DebugString()` helper, and it would satisfy the verb — but it dumps every span attribute. Attributes are unbounded in size and can carry request data (URLs, DB statements, custom tags), which makes them unsuitable for a value interpolated into a log line that fires once per malformed span. Both sites therefore log the identifying fields explicitly instead. `DebugString()` remains available for interactive debugging.

signal.title: [APM] Reduce allocations on the trace decode path
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Two independent allocation reductions on the trace-agent receive/decode path. **1. Intern strings directly from the payload (v0.4 decode).** `parseStringBytesRef` materialized a Go string for every value just to look it up in the payload's string table, discarding it on a hit. **2. Reserve `bytes.MinRead` beyond the body when buffering a request.** `reserveBodySize` reserved exactly `Content-Length`, but `io.Copy` bottoms out in `bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom`, which needs `bytes.MinRead` of spare capacity for the read that reports EOF. Also fixes two swapped godoc names on `parseStringBytes` / `parseStringBytesRef`. ### Motivation Both were found in a staging heap profile of the trace-agent receiver. `pprof -traces` showed `bytes.Buffer.Grow` and `bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom` both allocating on the same `copyRequestBody` path — i.e. twice per request. ### Describe how you validated your changes New tests and benchmarks in both packages: - `pkg/proto/pbgo/trace/idx/string_intern_test.go` — `TestAddBytesMatchesAdd` asserts `AddBytes` and `Add` are behaviourally equivalent, so no decode divergence is introduced. - `pkg/proto/pbgo/trace/idx/string_intern_bench_test.go` — intern benchmarks across hit rates, including a `HitRate0` control arm. - `pkg/trace/api/body_buffer_test.go` — `TestReserveBodySizeLimit` pins the `MaxRequestBytes` boundary (at / one over / absent / unparseable), confirming the `MinRead` padding does not leak into the size check. `TestCopyRequestBodyNoRealloc` asserts the body lands in the same backing array that was reserved, by identity, rather than counting allocations. - `pkg/trace/api/body_buffer_bench_test.go` — `BenchmarkCopyRequestBody` over two regimes: `SmallWarmPool` (ordinary traffic, shows the change is neutral, 0 allocs/op) and `LargeColdBuffer` (the regime that actually generates the bytes). Also run: full `pkg/trace/api` and `pkg/proto/pbgo/trace/idx` suites, and `bazel test //pkg/proto/pbgo/trace/idx:idx_test //pkg/trace/api:api_test` — all pass. **Time** (benchstat, n=10, Apple M4 Max darwin/arm64; only `span.go` differs between arms) | Benchmark | before | after | delta | |---|---|---|---| | `StringTableIntern/HitRate100` | 24.42µ ± 4% | 14.74µ ± 1% | −39.6% | | `StringTableIntern/HitRate90` | 27.90µ ± 3% | 18.90µ ± 1% | −32.3% | | `StringTableIntern/HitRate50` | 31.80µ ± 2% | 25.63µ ± 1% | −19.4% | | `StringTableIntern/HitRate0` | 35.32µ ± 5% | 34.40µ ± 0% | −2.6% | | `SpanUnmarshalConvertedStrings` | 107.80µ ± 1% | 86.15µ ± 1% | −20.1% | **Allocations** | Benchmark | before | after | delta | |---|---|---|---| | `HitRate100` | 1003 allocs / 48288 B | 4 allocs / 336 B | −99.6% / −99.3% | | `HitRate90` | 1005 allocs / 44.3KiB | 105 allocs / 9.1KiB | −89.6% / −79.4% | | `HitRate50` | 1005 allocs / 73.8KiB | 505 allocs / 54.2KiB | −49.8% / −26.5% | | `HitRate0` | 1007 allocs / 108.4KiB | 1007 allocs / 108.4KiB | ~ (identical) | | `SpanUnmarshalConvertedStrings` | 3607 allocs / 227.6KiB | 1231 allocs / 197.9KiB | −65.9% / −13.1% | **Throughput on the end-to-end span decode: 417.5 → 522.4 MiB/s, +25.1%.** ### Additional Notes

signal.title: Add concurrency test for flare archive name uniqueness
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? * Adds a test that races many goroutines through `getArchiveName()` in `comp/core/flare/helpers/builder.go`, asserting no two calls ever produce the same archive filename. * Update the changelog to include changes from #54911 No production code changes: #54911's PID+counter suffix already guarantees this, but it was only covered by a single-threaded, same-timestamp test (`TestGetArchiveNameIsUniqueWithinSameSecond`). This adds a companion test that exercises real concurrent callers instead. ### Motivation We considered reverting #54911 in favor of relying on a higher-precision timestamp alone, but a concurrency test proved that `time.Now()`'s effective resolution is not a reliable uniqueness mechanism on its own — even on Linux, concurrent goroutines can read the identical nanosecond value. #54911's PID+counter suffix is what actually guarantees uniqueness, so we're keeping it as-is and locking in the guarantee with a test that mirrors the real production race: the `/agent/flare` HTTP handler and the remote-config listener independently calling `Save()` around the same time. Jira: FLREM-148, FLREM-150 ### Describe how you validated your changes - `dda inv test --targets=./comp/core/flare/... --no-cache --race`, repeated multiple times, all passing.

signal.title: feat(serverless-init): add ProcessHooks for subprocess liveness tracking
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds a `*ProcessHooks` parameter (`OnAlive`/`OnDead`) to `mode.RunInit` and its internal `execute()`, so a caller can be notified when the spawned user process starts and exits. `mode.Conf.Runner` is dropped for init-container mode — its field type (`func(*serverlessLog.Config) error`) can no longer match `RunInit`'s new two-argument signature, so `main.go` switches from calling `modeConf.Runner(logConfig)` to `cloudService.Run(modeConf, logConfig)`, which already exists on the `CloudService` interface and produces identical behavior for every existing cloud service (sidecar → `RunSidecar`, init-container → `RunInit` with `nil` hooks). Also adds `cloudservice.MicroVM`, a `CloudService` implementation for AWS Lambda MicroVMs, and a `LifecycleContext` type carried on `TracingContext.LifecycleCtx`: - `GetTags` parses `DD_AWS_MICROVM_IMAGE_ARN` for `region`/`account_id`/`image_name` (falling back to `"unknown"` for any field it can't parse). - `GetEnhancedMetricTags` derives base/usage tag sets from those tags. - `Init` reads a `LifecycleContext` (metric/log flushers, trace-tag/log-tag setters, flush timeout, sidecar flag) and constructs + starts the lifecycle hook server. - `Run` spawns the user process via `mode.RunInit`, binding `ProcessHooks.OnAlive`/`OnDead` to the lifecycle server's child so its `/ready` check reflects real liveness. Sidecar mode is fatal for MicroVM — there's no child process to track, so `/ready` would silently return 503 forever instead of surfacing the misconfiguration. - `Shutdown` stops the lifecycle server within a bounded timeout so in-flight `/suspend`/`/terminate` requests can complete before the metric/trace agents tear down. - MicroVM supports both amd64 and arm64 (every other cloud service here is amd64-only). `MicroVM` is **not yet reachable**: `GetCloudServiceType` still doesn't know about it, so nothing in the running agent changes yet. Also fixes review feedback from Copilot on this PR: - `mode/initcontainer_mode.go`: `hooks.OnDead`'s defer was registered only inside the `hooks.OnAlive != nil` branch, and after `OnAlive()` ran. An `OnDead`-only hook never fired, and `OnDead` wouldn't fire if `OnAlive` panicked. Now deferred unconditionally right after `cmd.Start()` succeeds. - `main.go`: fixed a non-gofmt-compliant import grouping. - `cloudservice/microvm_test.go`: reworded stale `/launch` references (test names, a path variable, assertion messages) to `/run`, matching the route actually under test. ### Motivation The upcoming MicroVM `CloudService` needs to know whether the customer's process is currently alive so its lifecycle server can answer `/ready` correctly — there's no other signal available once `cmd.Start`/`cmd.Wait` are called deep inside `mode.execute()`. `ProcessHooks` is the minimal hook point for that. `MicroVM` is the core piece of the MicroVM integration: everything needed to answer the lifecycle server's HTTP hooks and track the user process's liveness, in one type that satisfies `CloudService` end-to-end. This is the split of #53036 (`tianning.li/microvm-07-microvm-service-wiring`). Originally planned as 5 independently-reviewable PRs; PR 2 (MicroVM CloudService implementation) has since been merged into this branch, so **this PR now covers PRs 1 and 2 combined**: 1. ~~ProcessHooks plumbing in `mode` package~~ (this PR) 2. ~~MicroVM CloudService implementation (`cloudservice/microvm.go`)~~ (this PR) 3. MicroVM tags/metrics/arch tests 4. MicroVM lifecycle-server tests 5. main.go wiring + CloudService registration (tip == original #53036) ### Describe how you validated your changes ``` dda inv test --targets=./cmd/serverless-init/... ``` 299 tests pass (4 platform-skips). New coverage: - `initcontainer_mode_test.go` pins `OnAlive`/`OnDead` ordering (start → alive → wait → dead), the nil-hooks no-op path, `Conf.Runner` nil-for-init/non-nil-for-sidecar, and two regression tests for the OnDead/OnAlive fix above (`TestExecute_OnDeadOnly_OnAliveNil_StillFires`, `TestExecute_OnAlivePanics_OnDeadStillFires` — both fail against the pre-fix code). - `mode_windows_test.go` covers the updated stub signature. - `cloudservice/microvm_test.go` and `cloudservice/service_test.go` cover `MicroVM`'s tag parsing, enhanced-metric tags, init/run/shutdown, and selection priority over Cloud Run. ### Additional Notes No `BUILD.bazel` changes needed — `cloudservice/`, `mode/`, and `cmd/serverless-init/*.go` are Gazelle-excluded (see root `BUILD.bazel` lines 97-100).

signal.title: Report DDOT process state in the installer agent state
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds a `ddot_process_state` line to the agent state the fleet installer daemon reports through the remote-config client. It is set on the `datadog-agent` package entry, next to the existing stable/experiment version and config version. The state is read from `dd-procmgrd` over its socket (gRPC on a UDS on Linux, a named pipe on Windows — the `dd-procmgr` binary is never invoked) when the process manager supervises DDOT, and falls back to systemd on Linux / the service manager on Windows otherwise. This reuses `pkg/procmgr/coat`, which already performs exactly that collection for COAT telemetry and already carries a `ddot` entry in its service catalog; the new `Snapshot.ServiceProcessState` only maps a collected snapshot onto a reported value. Reported values: `running`, `starting`, `stopping`, `stopped`, `created`, `crashed`, `exited`, `failed` when procmgr supervises DDOT; `running` when the legacy systemd unit or Windows service is active; `not_installed` when DDOT is absent; `unknown` when procmgr owns it but is unreachable; and `""` only when nothing can be determined, so the backend can tell "not reported" from "no DDOT on this host". The probe is bounded (2s) and cannot fail a state refresh — it returns a string only, never an error. ### Motivation The update monitoring uses the reported agent state to decide whether an update succeeded. Now that DDOT can be updated on its own (version or config), the state had no way to express whether the DDOT process actually came back up afterwards. This matters because a broken DDOT does not end an experiment by itself: the core agent does not read `otel-config.yaml`, so the experiment agent stays healthy, and `dd-procmgrd` retries a failing child forever rather than giving up. The reported process state is therefore the only signal that can tell the backend not to promote. ### Describe how you validated your changes Unit tests: - `pkg/procmgr/coat/process_state_test.go` — every `pb.ProcessState`, both legacy supervisor modes, not-installed, procmgr-unreachable, installed-without-supervisor, unknown service ID. - `pkg/fleet/daemon/ddot_state_test.go` — the collector seam (nil collector, procmgr running/failed, systemd, not-installed) and a `refreshState` test asserting the field lands only on the `datadog-agent` entry. - `pkg/fleet/daemon/local_api_test.go` — the field round-trips through the local API `/status`. Ran: `bazel test //pkg/procmgr/coat:coat_test //pkg/fleet/daemon:daemon_test`, `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/proto/pbgo/core` (msgp round-trip), `bazel build //cmd/installer/...`, `dda inv linter.go`. Generated protobuf code is committed and `dda inv protobuf.generate` is a no-op on the tree. E2E — new `TestDDOTConfigFailureReportsFailedAndReverts` in the fleet config suite (Linux, runs in the existing `new-e2e-fleet-config` job with no CI wiring changes): 1. Install the agent and the `ddot` extension; assert DDOT healthy under `dd-procmgrd`, launched with the stable `otel-config.yaml`, reported as `running`. 2. Start a config experiment patching `/otel-config.yaml` with an invalid debug-exporter verbosity; assert the broken config reaches the experiment collector and DDOT is unhealthy. 3. Assert the reported `ddot_process_state` becomes `failed`. 4. Assert nothing promoted it: `experiment_config_version` still set, `stable_config_version` unchanged, stable config free of the bad value. 5. Mimic the backend reacting to that state by sending the revert task (`stop_experiment_config`). 6. Assert the revert landed: `experiment_config_version` cleared, `stable_config_version` never changed, stable `otel-config.yaml` restored byte-for-byte, DDOT healthy under `dd-procmgrd` on the stable config, reported state back to `running`. ### Additional Notes - **The failure state is `failed`, not `crashed`.** `CRASHED` exists in the proto and Go enums but the Rust process manager never emits it: `set_last_status` maps any non-zero exit or signal to `Failed`. - **`restart: on-failure` never gives up on DDOT.** With `restart_sec: 2`, backoff ×2 capped at 60s, and `start_limit_burst: 5` over a 10s window, attempts land at t≈0, 2, 6, 14, 30, 62… — never 5 within any 10s window, so DDOT loops `Failed → Starting → Failed` indefinitely and `dd-procmgrd` stays up. - Field 17 is new, so older backends skip it and newer backends see `""` from older agents. The msgp decoder skips unknown fields, so mixed-version marshalling is safe. - During a version experiment, `Installed`/`ProcmgrConfigured` are resolved from the daemon's own install root while the process state comes from the shared procmgr socket. That only affects the `unknown`-vs-`stopped` distinction; the running state stays correct, since the stable and experiment procmgr share one socket and the DDOT process definition filename is invariant (only `${DD_CONF_DIR}` differs).
signal.author: Stanislas167

signal.title: Convert Bazel test logs to test2json in-graph via aspect
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Converts each Bazel `test.log` to test2json **during** `bazel test`, via an aspect on `TestRunner` actions, instead of shelling out to a converter afterwards. `tasks/bazel.py` then concatenates the resulting fragments. It already parsed the BEP to collect `test.xml` for JUnit, so fragment locations are picked up in that same pass — there is one BEP parser, and `process-test-results` no longer invokes Bazel at all. ### Motivation The previous flow ran `bazel run //bazel/tools/testlogs_to_json` in `after_script` with a hand-maintained label/log manifest. Conversion is naturally per-test work, so it belongs in the graph where it is cached and parallelised alongside the tests. ### Design notes **Fragment discovery comes from the BEP, not from filenames.** The aspect publishes a `test2json` output group; `targetCompleted` events carry that group, and its `fileSets` resolve through `namedSet` events to concrete file URIs. Nothing re-derives the aspect's naming scheme, so there is no filename contract between Starlark and Python. Outputs still in the remote cache report `bytestream://` rather than `file://`, so resolution falls back to the exec-root-relative path the BEP reports alongside. **Merging is not a Bazel action.** An earlier iteration expressed it as one, which was unsound: the rule declared only the BEP as an input and discovered fragments by globbing `bazel-out` at execution time, so nothing ordered it after the fragments, its cache key ignored their contents, and it required `no-sandbox` to run. After the aspect, aggregation is plain byte concatenation of newline-terminated JSONL, which does not warrant an action. **No post-test Bazel invocation.** This sidesteps configuration parity. The merge runs in `after_script`, where matching the test invocation's configuration would have meant threading per-job flag sets through CI — including a meaningless `--collect_code_coverage` for the coverage job, since `bazel coverage` implies it and it is configuration-affecting. **The Bazel label, not the Go import path, is the test2json package.** `dd_agent_go_test` emits several configured `go_test` targets for one Go package under different build-tag sets; collapsing them to one import path makes UTOF report distinct runs as retries of each other. ### Configuration `--config=test2json` enables the aspect and requests its output group. Bazel's `coverage` command inherits `test` options, so the `test:` lines cover both. No `--remote_download_regex` is needed: `--output_groups=+test2json` makes fragments top-level outputs, which `--remote_download_outputs=toplevel` already downloads. ### Possible drawbacks / Trade-offs Conversion is now on the critical path of the test invocation rather than in `after_script`, adding one small action per test target. In exchange those actions are cached and shared, so re-runs with cache hits do no conversion work at all. ### Describe how you validated your changes Local runs on macOS arm64, comparing against the previous manifest-based converter as the baseline: - **Output equivalence** — semantically identical to the manifest converter on the same BEP (104 events; the only differences across runs are wall-clock durations embedded in `--- PASS:` text). - **Failing tests** — a deliberately failing target still publishes its `test2json` group, and its `fail` events reach the merged output. Tests execute exactly once; making the aspect depend on `test.log` does not cause double-runs. - **Remote cache** — after `bazel clean`, with 108 remote cache hits and 9 of 10 tests served from cache, all 10 fragments materialised under `--remote_download_outputs=toplevel`. This rules out local action-cache re-materialisation masking the result. - **Multiple actions per target** — under `--runs_per_test=2`, two targets produced 4 uniquely named fragments, all reaching the merged output, with UTOF reporting them as retries. - **`bazel coverage`** — publishes the `test2json` group with only the `test:` config lines present. - **Failure path** — a BEP from a run without the aspect produces an actionable error rather than an empty result. - Unit tests for the aspect converter; `buildifier --lint=warn`, `gofmt` and `ruff` clean. CI will exercise the five reporting jobs (linux amd64/arm64, macOS amd64/arm64, coverage) on real `//...` invocations.

signal.title: feat(notableevents): add macOS shutdown-cause notable event
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds a macOS notable event that reports **why the previous boot ended**, recovered after the fact from the PMU rather than observed live. On Apple silicon, PMU/PMIC driver services publish an `IOPMUBootFaultInfo` IORegistry property: an array of short ASCII tokens naming the fault conditions that preceded the last power-off. This PR reads that property, classifies the tokens, and emits one notable event per boot when the classification is a fault. Five fault classes are covered, spanning the whole dictionary of 80 known tokens — 59 of which are faults: | Class | Title | Tokens | Example families | | ---------- | ------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------- | | `thermal` | macOS overheated shutdown | 14 | `ot`, `sochot`, `ntc_shdn` | | `power` | macOS power fault shutdown | 29 | `uv`, `ov`, `oc`, `buck`, `pgood` | | `crash` | macOS crash shutdown | 6 | `crash` | | `watchdog` | macOS watchdog timeout shutdown | 5 | `timeout` | | `hardware` | macOS hardware fault shutdown | 5 | `spmi`, `sgpio`, `fault`, `otp_crc` | - **Native reader** (`shutdown_cause_iokit_darwin.{c,h}`) walks the IOService plane, flattens every `IOPMUBootFaultInfo` array into a single `0x1f`-separated token sequence, and dedups as it writes — so no Core Foundation type crosses the cgo boundary. The whole plane is walked rather than matching a class because the publishing class is PMIC-specific and varies by Mac model, and IOKit cannot match on a property key alone (`kIOPropertyMatchKey` matches key *and* value). - **Classifier** (`shutdown_classify_darwin.go`) maps a token to its *family* (prefix before the first comma, a declared underscore family, or the whole token) and the family to one of five classes, resolved by fixed precedence: **thermal → power → crash → watchdog → hardware**. Thermal wins deliberately: a machine collapsing from heat also asserts reset, crash and power lines, and the event that matters most must not be titled as a crash. - **Event shape** (`format_darwin.go`) — `EventType` is the constant `"System shutdown fault"` so consumers can filter shutdown causes on one value; the class varies the title and message only. The payload reports every token observed *plus* the families and the fault subset the classifier acted on, so a reader sees both the raw evidence and what the verdict was based on: ```json "macos_shutdown_cause": { "source": "IOPMUBootFaultInfo", "classification": "thermal", "primary_family": "ot", "families": ["ot", "sochot"], "tokens": ["ot,tdie_overtemp", "ot,tsns_overtemp", "sochot,reset_in_3"], "fault_tokens": ["ot,tdie_overtemp", "ot,tsns_overtemp", "sochot,reset_in_3"], "boot_uuid": "…", "boot_time": "2026-08-11T09:55:21Z" } ``` - **Dedup is boot-scoped.** Identity is `shutdown:<bootUUID>:<sortedFaultTokens>`, hashed under a new `macos-shutdown-v1:` event-ID prefix. Both halves are load-bearing: the boot UUID alone says nothing about *what* was read, and the token set alone is identical across boots — a Mac that overheats every afternoon would emit one ID forever and be deduplicated into silence. Tokens are sorted first because PMU enumeration order is not stable (measured: two triggers with an identical fault set reported the groups in different order). - **Storage.** A new `ShutdownCause` bookmark field records the examined boot *whether or not* an event was emitted, so a cleanly-rebooting Mac does not re-read the property on every Agent restart. It is the primary guard rather than the `Acknowledged` map, which prunes after 30 days or 4096 entries — a Mac up longer than that would otherwise re-emit. The check runs **once per collector lifetime**, before the first directory scan, and is retried from the reconcile tick when it could not commit. It reads the property as an ordinary user (no root needed; system-probe runs as root regardless), and the whole feature is gated behind the existing `notable_events.enabled` setting, which defaults to `false`. **No benchmarks, deliberately.** There is no steady-state cost to measure: the IOService walk happens once per collector lifetime, is bounded at 16 services, and short-circuits as soon as every distinct token is accounted for. It is not on any per-event, per-scan or per-tick path. **Bookmark schema version stays at 1, deliberately.** `Load()` and `validateDarwinBookmarkState()` both require exact equality, so bumping to `2` would fail every existing v1 bookmark as corrupt — which resets state and re-baselines, discarding pending undelivered crash events on every upgraded host. `ShutdownCause` is `omitempty` with a nil zero value, so v1 bookmarks deserialize with no migration. Relatedly, `types.IsEventID()` had to learn the new prefix in the same change: a `macos-shutdown-v1:` ID written under the old single-prefix check would fail validation on the next `Load()` and wipe the bookmark, silently losing every pending crash event. ### Motivation [https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/WINA-3040](https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/WINA-3040) **A hard shutdown kills the Agent before it can report why.** Whether the machine overheated, lost a power rail, asserted its CRASH line, tripped a watchdog or hit a hardware fault, the Agent is gone before it can say so — the cause has to be recovered from the PMU on the next boot, or it is never recovered at all. All five fault classes are in scope here; thermal is one of them, not the point of the feature. **Predecessor: macOS app crash notable events (#54084).** This builds directly on it, reusing its bookmark, its `Pending`/`Ack` delivery contract and its at-least-once semantics unchanged — a second event *source* on that pipeline, not a second pipeline. It complements rather than replaces it: #54084 reports `.ips` files, which are written by a *running* OS about a *running* process, so a PMU-forced power cut leaves no `.ips` at all. The one adjacent artifact that does exist, `.shutdownStall` spindumps, records a *stalled* shutdown, not its cause. Everything else was surveyed and rejected: `pmset -g log` carries no cause data (25,117 lines grepped, nothing), `nvram -p` has no shutdown-cause variable, `ioreg -rc IOPMrootDomain` has no such property, `last -x reboot` is empty, and the `AppleSMC: Previous shutdown cause: <N>` unified-log line that Intel Macs emit **does not exist on Apple silicon**. Without this, a machine that overheated or lost a power rail badly enough to be cut off is a silent gap in the fleet record. `kern.shutdownreason` is **deliberately not read** — not as a source, not as a fallback, not as payload. It is the same PMU data flattened into an 80-byte-capped string, and it was already destroying data on an ordinary clean shutdown of the test machine: the cap was hit in 4 of 6 measured boots, always cutting *mid-token* and synthesising fault names that do not exist (`crash,crash`, `btn_rst,btn`, `rst_in,reset_in_1_d`). Absence of a token from that sysctl carries no information at all. The tradeoff is accepted and known: the sysctl also carries application-processor tokens (`ap_restart`, `ap_panic`) that `IOPMUBootFaultInfo` does not, and this PR gives those up rather than add a second parsing path and a second failure mode. ### Describe how you validated your changes **Unit tests — 240 tests pass in `pkg/notableevents`** (verified locally on the branch head with `dda inv test --targets=./pkg/notableevents/...`). Classifier tests deliberately use **payloads measured from real hardware** as fixtures rather than invented ones: | Pattern | Tokens (distinct union) | Emits | | ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | A — clean shutdown | `target_off_restart`, `wdog,reset_in_1`, `rst_in,reset_in_1_deassert` | no event | | B — `sudo reboot` | `wdog,reset_in_1`, `rst_in,reset_in_1_deassert` | no event | | C — button/force restart | + `rst`, `btn_rst,btn_seq_reset`, `crash,crash0_in` | `crash`, `fault_tokens = ["crash,crash0_in"]` | Also covered: the full 80-token dictionary maps to exactly one family each with the asserted **59 fault / 21 benign** split (14 thermal, 29 power, 6 crash, 5 watchdog, 5 hardware) — this pins a typo in the family map that would otherwise silently misclassify; class precedence in every pairing; unknown *suffix* within a known family (`ot,some_future_sensor`) still classifies thermal, which is the prefix contract; permuted group order yields an identical event ID; benign-token exclusions are dead-weight-free (each is in the measured dictionary *and* would otherwise be a fault); every classification fits the wire limit; malformed and oversized payloads are rejected. Collector tests cover the delivery contract end to end: one event per boot; `Start()` → `Close()` → `Start()` yields one event, not two; same boot UUID after Ack yields nothing; a *different* boot UUID with the same tokens yields a new event; a saturated pending queue **defers** rather than records, because recording the boot would be final and the fault cannot be reproduced by a later boot; a `Save` failure leaves nothing pending and is retried; a check blocked by an in-flight bookmark commit is retried from the reconcile tick rather than stranded for the process lifetime; reader failure, absent property and untrusted payload all leave crash-report collection unaffected; a v1 bookmark with no `shutdown_cause` key loads without being treated as corrupt. **Manual QA on real hardware.** `Mac17,9` / M5 Pro / macOS 26.5.2 (`25F84`), SIP enabled, no `boot-args`. **Six real boot sessions** executed one trigger at a time — the property is destroyed by the next reboot, so the runs could not be batched — with an immediate capture script per boot: `sudo reboot`, Control-Command-Power force restart, power button held ~10s, a deliberately stalled shutdown ended by the power button, the same stall resolved via Try Again → Force Quit, and a battery run-down. Three distinct payloads were observed across six distinct boot UUIDs, verified byte-identical by MD5, reverting to pattern A after a clean shutdown. That establishes the load-bearing premise: **the property is a live, event-driven, self-clearing signal, not a constant** — which is what validates both the read path and the boot-UUID dedup key. **How to reproduce a fault event yourself — the `crash` class, on demand.** One fault class is reproducible at will on Apple silicon, so a reviewer can exercise the whole path end to end without waiting for real hardware trouble. A force restart asserts the AP's CRASH line, which emits `crash,crash0_in`: 1. Enable the feature — it is off by default: ```bash # datadog.yaml notable_events: enabled: true ``` 2. Clear any prior bookmark so the check is not skipped as already-examined, and note that the file is root-owned: ```bash sudo rm -f /private/var/db/datadog-agent/notable-events/bookmark.json ``` 3. Record the current boot identity and the pre-restart payload, for comparison: ```bash sysctl -n kern.bootsessionuuid ioreg -l -w 0 | grep IOPMUBootFaultInfo ``` 4. Force restart: hold **Control-Command-Power** until the screen blanks. (Holding the power button ~10s, or ending a stalled shutdown with the power button, both produce the same payload — see the resolution caveat in Additional Notes.) 5. After the machine boots, confirm the PMU now reports the crash token. Expect pattern C — `rst`, `btn_rst,btn_seq_reset`, `target_off_restart`, `crash,crash0_in`, `wdog,reset_in_1`, `rst_in,reset_in_1_deassert`: ```bash ioreg -l -w 0 | grep IOPMUBootFaultInfo sysctl -n kern.bootsessionuuid # must differ from step 3 ``` 6. Start the Agent and system-probe, and confirm the event: ```bash sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.agent sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.sysprobe sudo cat /private/var/db/datadog-agent/notable-events/bookmark.json | jq . ``` Expect a `shutdown_cause` object whose `boot_uuid` matches step 5, and a `pending` entry with a `macos-shutdown-v1:` ID, `"event_type": "System shutdown fault"`, title `macOS crash shutdown`, `"classification": "crash"`, and `fault_tokens` of exactly `["crash,crash0_in"]` — all six tokens appear in `tokens`, but only the crash one elected the class. 7. Confirm the dedup guard: restart the Agent without rebooting. No second event should be emitted, and `shutdown_cause.boot_uuid` should be unchanged. To verify the **negative** case, `sudo reboot` instead of step 4 (pattern B) or shut down cleanly from the Apple menu (pattern A). Both must produce a `shutdown_cause` record with **no** event — a clean shutdown emitting an event is the failure mode most worth catching, since `wdog,reset_in_1` is present on every ordinary shutdown. **`qa/rc-required` — why this needs RC validation.** The classes that matter most in the field cannot be triggered on any machine we control, and cannot be simulated at all: the property is written by the PMU at power-off and is read-only through every interface, with no writable backing store. Reproducing a genuine thermal, power-rail or hardware fault means real failing hardware. Virtualized macOS runners expose no PMU, so the property is simply absent there and CI can only assert graceful degradation. What RC deployment adds is a full end-to-end test on real hardware: that the notable event is actually emitted and delivered, and that its tags and payload arrive intact. The predecessor, #54084, carried the same label for the same reason. **What was NOT validated, and cannot be:** - **No thermal token has ever been observed on this machine** — not `ot,*`, not `sochot,*`, not `ntc_shdn`. The thermal classification is inferred from token names in the PMU's own declared dictionary (published as `info-fault_name-<N>` properties on the `pmu,spmi` device-tree nodes). This is a hard limit, not a gap in the testing: there is **no native way to fake a thermal shutdown cause**. The value is produced by the PMU at power-off and exposed read-only through every interface, with no writable backing store — `sysctl -w` refuses (read-only OID), there is no user-settable IORegistry path, no `nvram` variable, and a userspace `os_log` line would not carry the right sender image. Generating real heat was out of scope. **The thermal path should not be described as verified in any customer-facing text or release note.** - **The real IOKit read on CI.** macOS VMs expose no PMU, so the property is absent and the reader returns empty. No E2E test is added; on a virtualized runner one could only assert graceful degradation, which is worth having but would not be thermal coverage. ### Additional Notes **Known tradeoff — `crash` fires on user force-restarts.** Measured, not hypothetical: `crash,crash0_in` appeared in pattern C with no panic induced. The token means the AP's CRASH line was asserted, which a hard reset satisfies, so **every user-initiated force restart on this hardware emits a `crash`-classified event.** Accepted because a force restart is itself a signal that something went wrong badly enough that the user gave up on the machine, and the alternative — treating the family as benign — silently dropped genuine AP and hypervisor crashes. Two commitments follow: the message says "followed a CRASH signal from the processor" and never claims a kernel panic; and if force restarts dominate emitted volume, the fix is to split `crash,hyp_*` from `crash,crash*_in`, not to revert the family to benign. **Fault allowlist, not benign denylist.** Under a denylist, any Mac whose clean shutdown emits an uncatalogued token would raise a shutdown-fault event on *every boot*. A permanent false positive is noticed and distrusted; a missed rare fault is not. The cost is that a genuinely new fault token on unfamiliar hardware is dropped silently — mitigated by matching on the family *prefix*, so `ot,anything_new` still classifies thermal. **Two benign per-token exceptions** (`shutdownBenignTokens`), for tokens whose family is a fault but whose meaning is not: `buck_boot_charge` (booting after the battery charged from depleted, not a regulator failure) and `timeout,dblclick_timeout` (the power-button double-click window). Both produced a user-visible fault event on a machine that had not faulted. Scoped to these two deliberately — the other `buck_*` tokens name real regulator failures. Excluding one only changes the outcome when it is the sole evidence for its class. **Graceful degradation is strictly additive** — nothing here can block `Start()` or interfere with crash-report collection. Property absent → no event, debug log. IOKit failure → no event. `kern.bootsessionuuid` unreadable → skip the whole check, since without a dedup key an event could repeat on every Agent restart. `kern.boottime` unreadable → fall back to the current time and omit `boot_time`. Event over the wire limit → drop and warn, **never truncate a fault payload**, because a truncated one would be misleading. Save-failure and saturation warnings latch so a persistent condition warns once rather than on every reconcile tick, and are kept separate so neither can silence the other. **Bounds are derived from real hardware, and shared between C and Go so they cannot drift.** `DD_PMU_MAX_TOKENS_PER_SERVICE 88` and `DD_PMU_MAX_TOKEN_CHARS 53` come from the largest known real payload (80-token dictionary, longest token 35 bytes) plus margin — 10% on count, 50% on length — and the Go-side `maxShutdownTokens` / `maxShutdownTokenBytes` are derived from those same macros. `DD_PMU_MAX_SERVICES` is 16, matching how few PMU-publishing services exist in practice. A service exceeding its bounds is dropped and logged rather than failing the read; an oversized token is truncated rather than dropping its whole service; the walk stops early once every distinct token is accounted for, since no remaining service can contribute one that has not been seen. **Intel Macs silently emit nothing.** `IOPMUBootFaultInfo` does not exist there; `readPMUBootFaultInfo` returns `errShutdownCauseUnsupported` when `runtime.GOARCH != "arm64"`. The Intel path (SMC shutdown-cause code `-81` via `log show`, which needs root) is unimplemented and unvalidated — no Intel Mac available. Apple documents none of this property: `org:apple-oss-distributions` returns zero hits for both `IOPMUBootFaultInfo` and `info-fault_name`. Provenance is the device's own ADT table, community string dumps of the `AppleD2255PMU` kext, and independent confirmation of the prefix decodings in `hack-different/apple-knowledge`. The *read mechanism*, by contrast, is entirely public API: `IOServiceMatching`, `IOServiceGetMatchingServices`, `IOIteratorNext`, `IORegistryEntryCreateCFProperty`.

signal.title: [NETPATH-1122] Add baseline Dynamic Tests for CNM (deprecated version)
signal.text: <!--Please give us some feedback on your experience writing this PR ! https://app.datadoghq.com/forms/43db4c02-6837-400c-8083-692e141b1b88 !--> ### What does this PR do? Adds opt-in baseline Dynamic Tests for Cloud Network Monitoring (CNM). Baseline mode selects a small, representative set of paths directly from each CNM connection snapshot when full connection-monitoring Dynamic Tests are disabled. Traceroute must also be enabled in the system-probe configuration. If full connection-monitoring Dynamic Tests are enabled, they take precedence and the collector continues to use standard scheduling. ### Motivation Hosts without full Dynamic Tests currently have no included Network Path coverage for observed CNM traffic. Baseline mode provides limited recurring path visibility. The selector favors connections that are more useful for diagnosis while keeping resource use predictable: timeout, RTO, and retransmit observations rank ahead of healthy traffic, then higher-volume connections rank first. ### Design and key changes #### Snapshot selection - Reuses the existing connection eligibility filters before ranking. - Selects at most three unique paths from each complete CNM snapshot. - Ranks diagnostic observations first, then total sent and received bytes, with the stable path hash as the final tie-breaker. - Keeps only the best three candidates while scanning, so selection memory remains bounded and connections are not aggregated. - Reconsiders a repeated path only when its later observation has a stronger score. #### Data boundary Both CNM producers populate the same generic `ConnectionSignals` structure on `NetworkPathConnection`: normalized timeout count, RTO count, retransmits, sent bytes, and received bytes. These are raw connection observations rather than baseline-specific derived state. The baseline selector in `baseline.go` is the only layer that interprets those signals into the diagnostic and traffic-volume ranking dimensions. This keeps producer behavior equivalent without coupling the shared connection model to baseline policy. #### Scheduling and payloads Standard, baseline, and NetFlow paths share the collector's existing eligibility checks, path construction, scheduling telemetry, deduplication, interval, TTL, context limit, and rate limit. Baseline mode adds only the snapshot-ranking step before selected paths enter that common machinery. Baseline results are recurring Dynamic Tests and carry `dynamic_test_profile: "baseline"` in Network Path payloads so downstream consumers can distinguish them from standard tests. Baseline-only operation also enables the collector and its reverse-DNS dependency. Baseline mode and Dynamic Remote Configuration filters are compatible and independent: baseline mode controls snapshot ranking, while the effective local-plus-RC filter controls path admission. When an RC rule admits the winning baseline candidate, its configuration ID, source, and tags are preserved alongside `dynamic_test_profile: "baseline"`. #### E2E coverage Adds a packaged-Agent E2E suite that generates CNM host traffic and verifies through fakeintake that a Network Path event is emitted with the baseline profile. The existing Remote Config host-traffic suite and the new baseline suite now share one fixture. The fixture replaces the GHCR-backed HTTP container and runtime `curl` installation with Python standard-library HTTP and traffic generation, including readiness checks, cleanup, and failure logs. ### Manual validation Use this minimal `datadog.yaml` configuration: ```yaml network_config: enabled: true network_path: connections_monitoring: baseline_tests_enabled: true ``` Enable traceroute in `system-probe.yaml`: ```yaml traceroute: enabled: true ``` After generating outbound TCP traffic from the host, verify that Network Path events are emitted with `test_run_type: "dynamic"` and `dynamic_test_profile: "baseline"`. Up to three unique eligible paths should be selected from each CNM snapshot, subject to the existing collector filters and scheduling limits. ### Describe how you validated your changes - `bazel test //comp/networkpath/npcollector/impl:impl_test` - Added focused unit coverage for selection order, each diagnostic signal, sent/received byte derivation, repeated-path handling, configuration, producer signal mapping, payload serialization, and recurring scheduling cadence. - Added packaged-Agent E2E coverage for baseline Network Path events through fakeintake. ### Additional Notes The new configuration setting defaults to `false` and remains an internal rollout control omitted from generated `datadog.yaml` examples.

signal.title: fix(e2e/discovery): Wait for fixture services to listen before asserting
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Waits for each fixture service to actually be listening on its port before the discovery assertions start. `startServicesFromList` issued `systemctl start` and returned. The units are `Type=simple`, so that returns at fork — long before the application has booted and called `listen()`. The 3 minute per-service budget was therefore covering two unrelated things: the discovery pipeline, and the service's own startup. The pipeline part is bounded and deterministic: | Stage | Value | |---|---| | Discovery scan cycle (`discovery.service_collection_interval`) | 60s | | Minimum process age before a PID is queried (`discovery.service_collection_min_process_age`) | 60s | | Process check interval (`process_config.intervals.process`) | 10s | | Process must have existed in the previous check run | +1 cycle | | Test waits for ≥2 payloads | +2 cycles | A service that is already listening is reported within about 60s (next scan) + 20s (two process checks) = **80s**. That is exactly the maximum observed across passing runs, and the durations are identical run to run: `node-json-server` takes 60.00s / 30.00s / 80.00s / 50.00s in its four mode combinations, in both the passing retries and the passing halves of the failing jobs. The startup part is not bounded. Discovery only returns a service once the process has a listening socket, so each scan missed while a service is still booting costs a full 60s. With 180s − 80s = ~100s of slack, the assertions tolerate **one** missed scan (140s) and not **two** (200s). Waiting for the port keeps the 3 minute budget covering the pipeline only, and makes a fixture that fails to come up report itself as such — via the `dumpServiceDiagnostics` added in #54205 — instead of as an unexplained discovery timeout. ### Motivation DSCVR-621. Both failures behind that ticket were the fixture not running, not the discovery pipeline being slow, so raising the timeout would not have fixed either: - **job 1874204604 / `rails-svc`** — the rails process is absent from workloadmeta in three of the four debug dumps, while python and node are present in all four (including the two dumps from the `ProcessCollectionDisabled` variant, so the absence is real rather than a config artifact). In the one dump where it appears it is nine seconds old, about four minutes after `systemctl start`. It failed in all four mode combinations across ~20 minutes. So the service was not running for most of the job. Its failure cadence and cause are not established — nothing recorded the fixture's own output — but no assertion timeout helps a service that is not there. - **job 1890377724 / `node-json-server`** — the only matching process in workloadmeta is `npm exec json-server …` (`Comm: npm exec json-s`), which can never satisfy the test's matcher, since `matchProcess` requires `Args[0]`, `Exe` or `Comm` to equal `"node"` exactly. The process the test matches is the `node` grandchild npm spawns, which does not exist until npm has finished resolving. Its sibling `node-instrumented`, started in the same second, was discovered with complete service discovery data. Note that this change does not claim to make either failure pass. It makes the failure legible and correctly attributed, and stops the assertion budget being consumed by something it was never sized for. ### Describe how you validated your changes - `dda inv linter.go --targets=./test/new-e2e/tests/discovery` — clean. - `new-e2e-discovery` passes on this branch. - Every fixture honours `PORT`, so the ports in `servicePorts` match what each service binds: `python/server.py` reads `PORT`, `instrumented.py` calls into it, `node/instrumented/server.js` reads `process.env.PORT`, `json-server` is passed `--port 8084` explicitly, and `rails server` picks up `PORT`. - `ss` is available on these images — it is already used against them by `test/new-e2e/tests/agent-metric-pipelines/common/adp.go` and `test/new-e2e/tests/agent-platform/common/bound-port/unix.go`. Its `Local Address:Port` column prints as `0.0.0.0:<port>` followed by padding, verified on Ubuntu 22.04 / iproute2, which is why the match is on the port plus its trailing separator rather than a bare substring. A green run does not exercise the new code path meaningfully: the gate returns in a couple of seconds when the fixtures are healthy, which is the normal case. It confirms no regression rather than confirming the fix.

signal.title: [VULN-84904] fix(cluster-agent): require the local IPC token on admin API endpoints
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Hardens Cluster Agent API authentication by selecting exactly one credential per request and stopping immediately when validation fails. - Local administrative endpoints now require the local IPC token and no longer fall back to the cluster-wide DCA token. - Authentication decisions use r.URL.Path, preventing query-string slashes from changing path classification. - /api/v1/info/node/{nodeName} is correctly classified as a Node Agent endpoint. - Tests verify both response codes and that rejected requests never reach the wrapped handler. ### Motivation [VULN-84904](https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/VULN-84904). A failed local IPC-token check could fall through to DCA-token validation, allowing holders of the cluster-wide token to execute local administrative handlers despite receiving a 403 response. The path classifier also included query strings, enabling / characters in query values to misclassify administrative routes as external. Finally, the Node Agent’s node-info endpoint was missing from the external-route list, causing legitimate requests to be rejected. This change makes the authentication boundary explicit, terminal, and consistent with each endpoint’s intended caller. ### Describe how you validated your changes unit test #### e2e test All requests originated from inside a Node Agent pod, where the cluster-wide DCA token is mounted. Authentication failures should return only 403 with the 22-byte invalid session token response; any additional output would indicate that the rejected handler executed. | Request (DCA token unless noted) | Result | |---|---| | `GET /config` | 403, 22 B only — no config leaked | | `POST /flare` | 403, 22 B only — no flare produced | | `GET /config` + local IPC token | 200, 65803 B config — positive control | | `GET /config` + bogus token | 403, 22 B only | | `POST /api/v1/clusterchecks/rebalance?x=/y` | 403, 22 B only — dispatch state unchanged | | `GET /api/v1/endpointschecks/configs?x=/y` | 403, 22 B only | | `GET /api/v1/annotations/node/<node>?filter=a/b` | 200 — reverse-direction fix confirmed | | `GET /api/v1/info/node/<node>` | 200, kubelet/kernel/machineID | | `GET /version`, `/api/v1/cluster/id`, `/api/v1/tags/node/<node>` | 200 | | `GET /config` with no Authorization header | 401 `no session token provided` | | `POST /stop` | 403 in 10.6 ms, process untouched | C [VULN-84904]: https://datadoghq.atlassian.net/browse/VULN-84904?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNWRkNTljNzYxNjVmNDY3MDlhMDU5Y2ZhYzA5YTRkZjUiLCJwIjoiZ2l0aHViLWNvbS1KU1cifQ

signal.title: feat(numa-monitoring): add experimental NUMA monitoring module and check
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Adds a new experimental `numa_monitoring` system-probe module and a companion Agent core check that report per-container NUMA placement quality on Linux. - **eBPF collection** — a `sched_switch` tracepoint (`numa-monitoring-kern.c`) accumulates per-cgroup, per-NUMA-node scheduler runtime into a per-CPU hash map. - **Memory distribution** — `/proc/<pid>/numa_maps` is parsed for resident memory per NUMA node. - **resctrl** — where the host exposes resctrl monitoring, the probe reads LLC occupancy and total/local memory bandwidth for the top container cgroups. Group capacity is bounded by `numa_monitoring.max_resctrl_groups` (default 16), with rotation and cleanup, and foreign-ownership conflicts are counted rather than fought over. - **Derived scores** — `remote_ratio`, `placement_mismatch`, and `badness_score` are computed from the runtime/memory distributions. Capabilities are detected at runtime and the detected feature set drives which metrics are emitted, so a host lacking an event omits that metric rather than reporting a misleading zero (the wire model uses pointer fields to distinguish a real zero from an unavailable event). The module reports its state, architecture, NUMA topology, feature list, active/capacity group counts, and read-failure counters through `agent status`. Metrics submitted: | Metric | Tags | |---|---| | `system.numa.cpu.runtime_share` | container tags, `numa_node` | | `system.numa.memory.resident` | container tags, `numa_node` | | `system.numa.cache.llc_occupancy` | container tags, `resctrl_domain` | | `system.numa.memory.bandwidth.total` / `.local` / `.remote_estimated` | container tags, `resctrl_domain` | | `system.numa.remote_ratio`, `system.numa.placement_mismatch`, `system.numa.badness_score` | container tags | Disabled by default. Enable with `numa_monitoring.enabled: true` in `system-probe.yaml`; the check is then scheduled via the `_numa_monitoring` autodiscovery identifier. **Requirements** - **Linux kernel 4.18+.** The program calls `bpf_get_current_cgroup_id` (added in 4.18) and `bpf_get_numa_node_id` (4.10). `NewProbe` refuses to start below 4.18 with an explicit message rather than surfacing a raw verifier error. This was caught by KMT on `centos_7.9` (3.10), where the load failed with `invalid func unknown#80`. - **CO-RE/BTF.** The probe ships CO-RE objects only, with no runtime-compiled fallback, matching the `noisyneighbor` probe. Hosts where CO-RE is unusable cannot run this check. The Agent ships embedded BTF, which is what makes this viable. ### Motivation NUMA placement problems (remote memory access, split scheduling across nodes) degrade workload performance in ways that existing Agent metrics don't surface. This gives per-container visibility into how well a workload's CPU time and memory are co-located, on the hardware where the platform can report it. ### Describe how you validated your changes Unit tests added and run: - `pkg/collector/corechecks/ebpf/probe/numamonitoring` — numa_maps parsing, distribution/score math, counter-rate reset and unavailable-event handling, range-list parsing, cgo struct alignment vs. the eBPF types, capability matrices across four hardware profiles (intel-amd, vera-like, grace-like, no-monitoring), resctrl rates, and foreign-ownership/capacity-rotation/cleanup. - `pkg/collector/corechecks/ebpf/numamonitoring` — asserts the capability-dependent metric subset: present events are submitted, absent ones are asserted missing. - `comp/core/autodiscovery/listeners` — `TestStaticConfigSchedulesNUMAMonitoring`. - `pkg/system-probe/config` — module enablement from config. Because the collection code is Linux-only and this was developed on macOS, the Linux packages were cross-compiled with a cgo toolchain and the test binaries executed under Docker on `linux/arm64`; all tests pass. `go vet -tags test` for `GOOS=linux` is clean on both packages, and `gofmt` is clean. Not yet validated on real hardware: the eBPF program load, resctrl reads against a live `/sys/fs/resctrl`, and end-to-end metric submission all still need a run on an actual multi-node NUMA host (both an Intel/AMD box with RDT/MBM and an Arm host) — the capability matrices are covered only by table-driven unit tests. There is also no E2E/fakeintake test asserting the payloads arrive. ### Additional Notes - Marked experimental in the config template, the packaged `conf.yaml.default`, and the status output; metric names may change. - Bazel wiring covers the eBPF program suite and cgo godefs verification; `tasks/system_probe.py` target lists are updated to match. There is no runtime-compilation bundle: the flattened runtime source added 206 KB to the package on disk, and the `noisyneighbor` probe already established CO-RE-only as the convention. - **`static_quality_gates` is red and needs a threshold bump.** This feature adds 372,163 bytes on disk, but `static_quality_gate_agent_rpm_arm64` and `static_quality_gate_agent_suse_arm64` had only 11,498 bytes of headroom on `main` — those budgets were already saturated, so no new eBPF check of any size fits. Dropping runtime compilation cut the overage from 352 KB to ~150 KB; closing the rest is not achievable without removing the feature. This needs a bump via `manual_gate_threshold_update` or the exception process, from the gate owners rather than in this PR. - Per the repo's review guidelines, cross-component (system-probe ↔ Agent) and packaging changes like this are the class of change that mostly isn't exercised by E2E on PR branches, so this likely warrants `qa/rc-required`.

signal.title: [Backport 7.83.x]  [datasecurity] resolve autodiscovery configs before matching postgres scan connections
signal.text: Backport bd1766d0c0b2273d893eb042499c9968c79c61a4 from #55078. ___ ## What - `resolvePostgresConnection` now reads `GetAllConfigs()` (resolved configs) instead of `GetUnresolvedConfigs()`, so autodiscovery template variables (`%%...%%`) are substituted before matching. - Adds `GetAllConfigs()` to the autodiscovery `Component` interface (+ noop impl). ## Why Postgres checks configured through autodiscovery annotations (`ad.datadoghq.com/postgres.checks`) use template variables that are only substituted once a service is matched. The scan-task resolver previously read *unresolved* configs, so a templated instance such as: ```yaml instances: - host: "%%host%%" port: 5432 dbm: true ``` could never match a scan-task entity, whose `database_host_name` is the concrete resolved host. And even if it did, the resulting connection would target `host: "%%host%%"`, which is not connectable. Reading the resolved config fixes both: the host is concrete and matchable. ## Why Backport to 7.83.x is justified - Tested the agent on my local machine and everything works as expected when using static Postgres check configs. - Data Security is a new product that is not enabled anywhere yet, so the blast radius of this change is effectively zero as the provider is not started unless data_security.enabled is set to true (default is false) - The bug was spotted while testing with autodiscovery-generated Postgres check configs. Back-porting allows support of autodiscovery-generated Postgres check configs in the upcoming 7.83.0 release.

signal.title: fix(remoteagentregistry): canonicalize local metric help
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Makes Core Agent telemetry HELP text canonical when Remote Agent Registry (RAR) merges incoming Prometheus telemetry. The telemetry component records HELP text for metric families it creates in the normal `/telemetry` registry. When RAR receives a remote family with the same name, it uses that local HELP text when constructing the forwarded Prometheus descriptor. Remote-only families retain the remote agent's HELP text. ### Motivation Prometheus requires metric families that share a name to use identical HELP text. A remote agent can currently supply a different description for a metric also emitted by Core Agent, causing the combined telemetry gather to fail. The Core Agent definition is the authoritative local contract. This includes the Core Agent DogStatsD client byte counters added in #54381. The regression coverage verifies that Core Agent's `dogstatsd_client__bytes_sent` HELP wins over incompatible ADP text while retaining the ADP sample and authoritative `emitter` label. ### Describe how you validated your changes - `bazel test //comp/core/telemetry/impl:impl_test //comp/core/remoteagentregistry/impl:impl_test --test_output=errors` - `git diff --check` - Independent spec-compliance and code-quality reviews. `dda inv test --targets=./comp/core/telemetry/impl,./comp/core/remoteagentregistry/impl --timeout=120` and `dda inv linter.go --targets=./comp/core/telemetry/impl,./comp/core/remoteagentregistry/impl --timeout=120` were blocked before compilation by an internal dependency-mirror HTTP 403 for `github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/extension/healthcheckextension@v0.158.0`, which is in its mirror cooldown window. ### Additional Notes The canonical HELP catalog deliberately covers metrics created through the telemetry component's counter, gauge, and histogram factory APIs. It excludes `DefaultMetric` and opaque direct `RegisterCollector` registrations, which are not part of RAR's normal telemetry registry merge path.

signal.title: feat(ssi): last-TRUE-wins SSI matching
signal.text: ### What does this PR do? Unify SSI matching on a single last-TRUE-wins matcher: - **Static targets** (Helm / Operator / `datadog.yaml`) are reversed at construction so config first-wins is preserved. - **RC policies** keep wire order (catch-all first, exceptions after) and are last-TRUE-wins as-is. - Evaluation is static first, then RC, then SSI inject-all only when both are absent. A matched deny does not fall through. ``` SSI | static targets | RC | Decision off | — | none | nothing off | — | policies | last matching policy, else nothing on | none | none | everything on | none | policies | last matching policy, else nothing on | present | none | first (as in the yaml) matching target, else nothing on | present | policies | first (as in the yaml) matching target, else last matching policy, else nothing ``` Stacked on #55057. ### Motivation RC is already last-wins on the wire. Using the same matcher for static targets (by reversing them) avoids two matching modes. Static targeting is evaluated before RC so a remote deny cannot override an explicit local target. ### Describe how you validated your changes - [x] Unit tests: `./pkg/clusteragent/admission/mutate/autoinstrumentation` - [ ] E2E `TestSSISuite/TestRemoteConfig` (HelmTargetWinsOverRemoteDeny, LastMatchingRemotePolicyWins) ### Additional Notes `HelmTargetWinsOverRemoteDeny` now expects the helm python workload to **keep** SSI when an RC deny matches `targeted-namespace`. That inverts the parent PR, where remote-before-local made the deny win.

signal.title: [datasecurity] resolve autodiscovery configs before matching postgres scan connections
signal.text: ## What - `resolvePostgresConnection` now reads `GetAllConfigs()` (resolved configs) instead of `GetUnresolvedConfigs()`, so autodiscovery template variables (`%%...%%`) are substituted before matching. - Adds `GetAllConfigs()` to the autodiscovery `Component` interface (+ noop impl). ## Why Postgres checks configured through autodiscovery annotations (`ad.datadoghq.com/postgres.checks`) use template variables that are only substituted once a service is matched. The scan-task resolver previously read *unresolved* configs, so a templated instance such as: ```yaml instances: - host: "%%host%%" port: 5432 dbm: true ``` could never match a scan-task entity, whose `database_host_name` is the concrete resolved host. And even if it did, the resulting connection would target `host: "%%host%%"`, which is not connectable. Reading the resolved config fixes both: the host is concrete and matchable. ## Why Backport to 7.83.x is justified - Tested the agent on my local machine and everything works as expected when using static Postgres check configs. - Data Security is a new product that is not enabled anywhere yet, so the blast radius of this change is effectively zero as the provider is not started unless data_security.enabled is set to true (default is false) - The bug was spotted while testing with autodiscovery-generated Postgres check configs. Back-porting allows support of autodiscovery-generated Postgres check configs in the upcoming 7.83.0 release.

signal.title: CONTINT-5289 - retry reaching kubelet with HTTPS
signal.text: <!--Please give us some feedback on your experience writing this PR ! https://app.datadoghq.com/forms/43db4c02-6837-400c-8083-692e141b1b88 !--> ### What does this PR do? When setting up the kubelet client if we fail to reach it using HTTPS, we try to reach it using HTTP. In this case, when a component requests the global kubelet client, this one is configured with HTTP, try to set it up with HTTPS again. In case of failure to reach it with HTTPS, return the kubelet client set up with HTTP, this is fine we'll retry later. In case of real failure return an error, we don't want to continue, this is ok as anyway if we kept the old client we'll reach some errors at some point too. In case we succeed, we never retry anymore. ### Motivation users getting stuck with an HTTP connection due to transient error at start, now will benefit from HTTPS connection after some retry. ### Describe how you validated your changes unit test with mock kubelet that denies HTTPS at start then allows it and validate the new client using HTTPS afterward. ### Additional Notes

signal.title: [CWS] Buffer security profile v2 metrics in atomics
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Moves the remaining inline `statsdClient` **counter** emissions in `ManagerV2` (`pkg/security/security_profile/manager_v2.go`) onto the existing accumulate-in-atomics + flush-once-in-`SendStats()` pattern already used by the sample-refresh, event-filtering, insertion-error and per-`(source, event_type)` counters. Converted: | Metric | Was emitted from | Now | |---|---|---| | `security_profile_v2.tag_resolution.events_dropped` | `purgeStalePendingEvents` | `tagResolutionEventsDropped` atomic | | `security_profile_v2.tag_resolution.cgroups_expired` | `purgeStalePendingEvents` | `tagResolutionCgroupsExpired` atomic | | `security_profile_v2.cleanup.profiles_removed` | `cleanupPendingProfiles` | `cleanupProfilesRemoved` atomic | | `security_profile_v2.eviction.runs` | `evictUnusedNodes` | `evictionRuns` atomic | | `security_profile_v2.eviction.nodes_evicted_per_profile` | `evictUnusedNodes` | `evictionNodesEvicted` atomic | | `security_profile_v2.size_in_bytes` + `security_profile_v2.persisted_profiles` (tagged) | `sendPersistenceMetrics` | precomputed `persistenceMetrics` map keyed by `(format, storage_type, compression)` | The tagged persistence counters follow the `eventMetrics`/`initEventMetrics` precedent: a pre-populated map of atomic buckets with precomputed tag slices, so there's no locking or per-emit allocation on the persist path. The `security_profile_v2.tag_resolution.latency` distribution is intentionally left inline, since a distribution can't collapse into a single counter without losing the histogram. ## Motivation Keep metric reporting off the hot / ticker paths and consolidate emission in `SendStats()`, consistent with the rest of the manager. ## Describe how you validated your changes - `go build ./pkg/security/security_profile/` - `go vet ./pkg/security/security_profile/` All converted counters are untagged (or share the same tag set), so summing the accumulated values and emitting once per cycle is equivalent to the previous per-call emissions. ## Possible Drawbacks / Trade-offs Per-profile eviction and per-persist emissions are now aggregated per `SendStats` cycle rather than emitted individually; since they share identical tags this does not change the aggregated series. ## Additional Notes Draft for review. Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

As a result it could stop before every extra was resolved, silently dropping dependencies only reachable through two or more `pkg[extra]` hops, and for the common case of a package with no self-referencing extras it never converged at all, running all 10000 rounds while evaluating each wheel's generated `BUILD` file ([#​4039](https://redirect.github.com/bazel-contrib/rules_python/pull/4039)). - (pypi) Requirement `--hash=<algo>:<digest>` pins and Simple API `#<algo>=<digest>` URL fragments are now parsed for all hash algorithms instead of silently dropping everything except `sha256`.
